#7530. When hackers become sources: Inside the new craft of reporting on hacked data

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“You’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.”

Some consequential reporting of recent years has emerged thanks to what is normally defined as a “hack-and-leak,” a specific kind of cyberattack that results in the release of the information obtained by hackers. When Anonymous and allied collectives breached corporations and state agencies during the hacktivist wave of the 2010s, for instance, they turned stolen data into front-page news.

Reporters covering the invasion of Ukraine have frequently worked with documents pulled from Russian institutions by hackers of different allegiances. Hacktivists have breached surveillance vendors and spyware firms, granting journalists direct and exclusive access to the internal files of companies that sell to repressive governments. Ransomware gangs, cybercriminal groups, and state-affiliated hackers deposit fresh troves of hacked data on the open internet, or route it to the public through intermediaries like Distributed Denial of Secrets.

How are journalists responding to these reporting scenarios? For my research, recently published in Journalism Practice, I interviewed 10 journalists across the U.S. and Europe who work or have worked with hacked data. Some of them specialize in the coverage of cyber issues; others mainly focus on current affairs and global conflict. These journalists work for a variety of news outlets, from investigative reporting newsrooms to general interest outlets and technology brands, and have engaged with hacker sources at various levels.

The journalists I spoke with paint a picture of an emerging craft, rather than a settled method. Here’s some of what I found.

There are no fixed guidelines or established and shared practices on how to handle and report on hacked material in news reporting. Instead, the methods are being developed by practitioners on a case by case basis. One reporter who works for an investigative newsroom told me:

Hackers themselves are becoming increasingly strategic about their relationships with the press. One reporter following a specific cyber beat emphasized this:

“I’d say that [hackers] of all kinds love to flex and get credit. A lot of them don’t, but many absolutely do. I’m not sure if the desire to flex has increased, but you’ve definitely seen the maturity of some hackers in how they approach the media. It’s not just about posting things to Twitter like it might have been before.

That maturity means developing awareness of how a story will be framed and disseminated and calculating which journalist to approach. Hackers now may select their outlets of choice, matching a leak to the reporter who they think is capable of understanding the story and carrying it further.

There are different kinds of hackers, wearing different and/or multiple hats. Interviewees drew distinctions between financially motivated cybercriminals, whose leaks are often equivalent to extortion by other means, and state-affiliated actors, who may also pose as independent hacktivists to launder politically motivated leaks into credible coverage.

At the same time, some hackers or hacker collectives — like Phineas Fisher, known for his activist remit against surveillance companies — may act for political and public interest–oriented reasons, reaching out to journalists to expose wrongdoing, unethical issues, or crimes. Notoriously, though, hacking is not a field in which hats are worn straightforwardly: Identities, definitions and agendas, including mere trolling, may blur into one another.

Hacked material needs to be handled with a great deal of skepticism. When working with hacked sources, one journalist said, it’s a matter of “treating every dataset as if it has chlamydia.” But the verification techniques the journalists said they use — such as confirming that an email address exists in a company’s records, cross-referencing with known facts, or examining a file for signs of tampering — are fairly conventional. This type of reporting requires more disclosures, especially when a source’s identity can’t be established. One journalist working in this area said:

I think you should be very transparent about that in your reporting. You should say something like, “We don’t know who the source is; it could be the GRU [Russian Federation] or whoever, but we have confirmed that this data is real and this is what it shows.”

Declared openly, the uncertainty may become a meaningful part of the story itself.

Source protection is further complicated when it comes to hackers. Some interviewees extend the full protection they would give any source to hackers, refusing to assist law enforcement even if the source is a self-declared criminal. Others prefer to know as little as possible about their sources, framing the choice as harm reduction for both parties. As one journalist in my sample put it:

The less I know about these things, the harder it’s going to be for me to burn my source or to publish something that inadvertently turns out to be harmful to my source.

Reporters working exclusively with material already circulating online in cybercrime forums or other repositories on the web treat source protection as beside the point, because the origins of the information cannot be traced and because the material is in effect “out there.”

Beneath all of this sits the finding with the widest implications: Ethical decisions in this domain resist strict codification. No general rule can be written in advance, the reporters I spoke with suggested, and judgment in the individual case is the only workable guide. Is publishing hacked material justified? It depends on the specifics of the case at hand, one reporter told me.

I kind of think it all depends on what you’re exposing. Maybe it’s generally wrong to break into people’s computers and steal data, but if you’re exposing serious crimes, then I think it can be justified.

Interviewees described practical wisdom under pressure: the ability to read a specific situation and act appropriately n it, without having the opportunity to refer to an established code or checklist.

Newsrooms, meanwhile, may need to develop verification standards suited to information of illicit origin, transparency norms that treat uncertainty as something to disclose rather than paper over, and a shared language for the ethical judgments that journalists currently make case by case on their own.

Philip Di Salvo is a senior researcher and lecturer at the Institute for Media and Communications Management at the University of St. Gallen, Switzerland. Adobe Stock

#7527. GEO Isn’t A Distraction – AI Influence Doesn’t Show Up In Referral Data via @sejournal, @TaylorDanRW

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

GEO's value goes beyond referrals: AI answers shape buying decisions before a click, and ChatGPT visitors convert at nearly five times the search rate.

In her examination of website referral numbers, Marie Haynes suggests that GEO represents a misplaced investment for digital teams.

By reviewing data across 145 million sessions (over 100 websites), the article demonstrates that visits from ChatGPT represent less than one percent of the volume delivered by traditional Google search. The sample size is strong, but as with anything in SEO and organic visibility, mileage varies.

I did my own follow-up study looking at 108 million sessions from Jan. 1 to Nov. 2, 2026 (over 57 websites), and came to a similar finding that total AI traffic amounted to 0.66% of the total. This means that for every 1,000 users from search engines, (trackable) AI sends seven.

This does vary a lot between websites, with some seeing 20-25 AI users per 1,000, but the numbers are still relatively low.

The findings also reveal that people arriving from ChatGPT convert at about five times the rate of typical searchers, yet the conclusion maintains that marketing teams should ignore directly looking at optimizing for AI because Google still provides the vast majority of total sales.

While the recorded traffic numbers are accurate, the strategic conclusion rests on assumptions that fail to match the real habits of people who use modern AI tools.

Judging the business value of conversational tools by counting immediate site visits applies an outdated measurement system to a new information environment, as users are behaving differently with AI interfaces than what they have done traditionally with a standard search engine.

Neglecting GEO as a principle because incoming sessions appear small ignores the fact that conversational answers shape purchasing choices long before any link receives a click, while it also overlooks the commercial value of visitors who convert at remarkable rates.

The foundation of the argument depends entirely on website analytics sessions, which register zero value whenever an answer engine satisfies an inquiry without sending a person to an external domain. This reporting method breaks down because conversational platforms exist to answer complex questions without requiring people to browse through lists of web pages.

As documented in coverage on zero-click search dynamics, automated summaries satisfy informational demand directly on the platform and reduce traditional outbound journeys. When a procurement team researches software packages or a shopper looks for reliable touring bicycles, the entire comparison takes place inside the conversation window.

A company buyer might spend half an hour discussing system security, pricing tiers, and practical trade-offs among several competing vendors. If an engine explains your product with precision and presents it as a sensible choice, that buyer needs no immediate link click because the required knowledge is already in hand.

Several days later, that same individual opens a standard web browser, searches for your brand name, and completes a demonstration booking. The analytics platform credits standard organic search with the resulting transaction, reinforcing the mistaken belief that Google generated the entire customer journey when the real choice occurred inside the chat interface.

Ignoring conversational optimization because direct referral traffic seems negligible resembles dropping brand sponsorship because people decline to click on road signs. Concentrating solely on immediate referral links creates an analytical blind spot, because the work of optimizing for generative engines focuses on brand placement within the data sources that modern engines trust.

Analyses into GEO principles highlight how modern engines prioritize clear entity relationships and structured knowledge over traditional ranking signals. If an engine ignores or misrepresents your company during this silent research phase, that eventual conversion via traditional search will never take place.

See also: The AI Search Metrics I Use To Track Client Pipelines

The research by Haynes contains a striking detail, showing that visitors arriving from ChatGPT converted at almost 14% while standard search visitors converted at 3%. Dismissing this huge performance gap simply because total volume remains modest values raw visitor numbers over genuine commercial results, which conflicts with sound marketing economics.

Standard search traffic contains substantial waste, including accidental clicks and casual browsing from people who possess no intention of purchasing anything. Pouring effort into capturing massive organic volume often produces diminishing returns, filling site logs with casual readers who quickly leave without taking action. In contrast, industry reports on B2B citation behavior confirm that buyers engaging with generative syntheses click-through primarily to confirm factual details and evaluate final purchase considerations.

A person who conducts an interactive evaluation inside a conversational engine and then follows an outbound reference link exhibits exceptional commercial intent, having already moved past basic research to understand product strengths and weaknesses.

For B2B suppliers, high-value consultants, and specialized retailers, aggregate visitor volume remains an empty vanity metric. A firm that gains several enterprise clients from a modest stream of qualified conversational referrals earns far more profit than one attracting thousands of random visitors who generate nothing.

Directing resources toward an audience that converts at such remarkable rates represents sensible commercial planning, so the right response to a 5x conversion advantage is to study the reasons behind that success and ensure that your organization appears whenever serious buyers seek recommendations.

See also: AI Mode Sends A Different Visitor. Your Website Wasn’t Built For Them

The structure of the internet continues to transform, and the analysis correctly notes that autonomous systems will alter future business activities across digital channels.

Turning away from GEO because referral numbers appear modest misunderstands where commercial decisions occur today. AI tools have reshaped how shoppers and corporate teams research and purchase products, and the influence of this behavioral change remains invisible on standard traffic dashboards even as it appears within the exceptional conversion rates of those who visit.

Treating generative engines as an unimportant diversion surrenders your presence at the point of decision, leaving the field open to competitors who recognize that influence matters far more than traditional clicks.

#7525. Will AI slop overwhelm creators? Mark Rober isn’t worried–but his team is using AI as a “thought partner” in production

Mark Rober told Business Insider he thinks his content has a “moat” that will keep it safe from being affected by the AI slop deluge.

But, at the same time, he’s said his team is using generative AI as a “thought partner” for writing, and that it can make “the perfect meal” for students using his Class CrunchLabs modules.

With BI, Rober addressed creators’ anxiety about AI-generated videos encroaching on the watch time that should go to their genuine content.

“Do you want to see a simulation of someone dunking a basketball with a sick trick, or do you want to see someone actually do it?” he told BI. “The fact that [viewers] know it’s real is what makes it crazy.”

He said creators should be reassured that “[o]ur brains developed for hundreds of thousands of years with human connection,” and viewers want “real and authentic” content filmed by people who interact with the world around them.

He also added that people need to retain their cognitive skills instead of just ChatGPTing everything. Both creators and viewers should investigate things themselves, using their own human brains.

“Curiosity is so important in this new age of AI,” he said. “It means you just have a lifetime of learning, versus like, ‘Oh, this thing knows the answer, so who cares?'”

But, again, Rober has implemented AI across his processes. This past June, he told The Information that AI “has the power to really adapt” educational settings.

“Basically what we’re doing with Class CrunchLabs is we’re making great ingredients, really fresh ingredients, and then AI can be like, ‘Hey, I have three kids in my class who are challenged this way, and they’re not great at reading, but these ones are. We’ve already covered this stuff.’ And it could take those ingredients and make the perfect meal for your class,” he explained. “I think it’s gonna be very good at that.”

He said that on the creator side, “I think it would allow me to scale myself in certain ways. We’re certainly using it as a thought partner on writing, on some thumbnail stuff.”

Like he did with BI, Rober said that in science content specifically, viewers probably want something real instead of something LLM’d. “I think it remains to be seen what the public’s appetite is for just pure AI-generated content,” he said. “I would think in science, you actually want to see the lava melt through the thing, versus it just being completely fake. But we’ll see.”

We’ve written before about how big tech platforms like YouTube have found themselves in a tricky catch-22: They want to make money off the AI bubble (uh oh), but as they roll out more generative tools and push creators to use them, they end up combating endless amounts of slop pumped out by those very same tools.

With Rober and other creators, we see something similar: They feel their content is safe from AI content made by other people, but also use AI in their processes, in the name of “scaling” or “ideating” or streamlining and cost-lessening production.

Rober’s team is using AI in its writing process, and a script is the foundation of long-form, educational YouTube content like his. Is the vibe just that viewers won’t care, so long as no fully AI-generated video makes it into an upload? Intriguing…

#7524. Two out of five Americans regularly get their news on Facebook

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Despite what my Facebook feed looks like, the platform’s not just for AI fruit videos and birthday posts.

According to data from the Pew Research Center published Monday, 40% of adults in the United States regularly get their news from Facebook.

That’s up from 36% in 2020, signaling the continued stability of the platform as a news source — a trend that the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism observed in its Digital News Report this year. As we reported in June, people around the world are increasingly abandoning news websites for social media.

The Center surveyed 5,600 U.S. adults in late August as part of its American Trends Panel, and asked respondents several questions about their news and social media habits. Pew did not give respondents a definition of “news,” instead letting them use their own understanding of the term when they filled out the survey. More than half (59%) said that they get news from social media “often or sometimes,” but only 19% actually prefer social media as a place to get news.

Of Facebook news consumers, 33% are men and 49% are between the ages of 30 and 49. The platform is most popular for women (47%), Hispanic Americans (51%), Americans with a high school diploma or less (46%), and Republicans (43%).

Regular news consumption among American users has increased on nine of the 12 social media platforms that Pew studied, including YouTube, Instagram, TikTok, X (Twitter), Reddit, Nextdoor, LinkedIn, and WhatsApp. News consumption has either dropped or stayed the same on Rumble, Truth Social, and Bluesky.

The second-most regularly used platform among American adults is YouTube (34%), followed by Instagram (23%), TikTok (20%), and X (10%). YouTube news consumers are more likely to be male (41%), between ages 18 and 29 (39%), and identify as Black (47%) or Asian (53%). Republicans (35%) and Democrats (36%) are equal YouTube news consumers.

The most regularly used platform for news among young adults is Instagram (43%), followed by Facebook (40%), TikTok and YouTube (both 39%), and X and Reddit (both 18%).  The Center found that 20% of U.S. adults now regularly get their news on TikTok, up from 3% in 2020. Of TikTok users, 53% reported getting news regularly on the platform. Nextdoor users are also increasingly turning to the neighborhood forum app for information. In 2026, 45% of Nextdoor users reported regularly getting news from the app, up from 23% in 2022.

#7521. The Wall Street Journal’s new AI tool, “Doppler,” forecasts the issues that will shape the midterm elections

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Ahead of Election Day, the tool has ingested 25 million TikTok videos and 500,000 podcasts to gain new insight into U.S. voters.

More than 100 million voters are expected to cast ballots in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

In recent election cycles, political reporting based on voter polling has drawn criticism, prompted scrutiny, and found defenders. As the debate over the value of polling continues, The Wall Street Journal is exploring new ways to cover public opinion and break out of traditional horse race political coverage.

In late September, the Journal published its first story using Doppler News AI, a custom tool built to help expand the publication’s midterms coverage. So far, Doppler has ingested more than 25 million TikTok videos, roughly 500,000 podcast episodes, and thousands of Instagram videos and cable news segments. The Journal uses the tool to monitor trends across the internet and to identify voter priorities, concerns, and sentiments that traditional polling might miss.

RELATED ARTICLEHow The New York Times uses a custom AI tool to track the “manosphere”Andrew DeckFebruary 11, 2026“We’re not trying to predict the election, but people encounter politics through a lot of different lanes: culture, work, money, family, community. We wanted to tap into that and listen in on those conversations,” said Aja Whitaker-Moore, the deputy editor-in-chief of the Journal. “We’re taking a massive set of information…and telling you, from a statistical standpoint: ‘Here’s what people are talking about. Here are the questions they’re asking. Here are the places where those conversations are happening.'”

Other newsrooms have leaned on AI “visibility tools” in the past to support their reporting. That includes using large language models (LLMs) to transcribe and summarize “manosphere” podcasts, school board meetings, and local talk radio shows. But Doppler goes further.

Rather than using AI-generated summaries to generate leads or help beat reporters monitor online content more efficiently, the Journal uses Doppler to conduct large-scale AI analyses quickly — and publishes those insights for readers.

So far, analyses produced by Doppler have led to four major midterms stories in the Journal, with more expected to run before Election Day. For now, each story requires a custom treatment, with engineers and data journalists working alongside the D.C. politics team to refine the methodology, toggle on and off different features, and audit the results.

“The tool is only as good as the questions that you ask it,” said Whitaker-Moore. The Journal holds a weekly editorial meeting leading up to Election Day to workshop story angles and find new threads to explore.

A new in-house AI tool lets WSJ reporters analyze trends in online conversation to help understand the political mood of the country ahead of the midterm elections. A previous post paired a visual of TikToks from across the internet with a headline that identified them as conservative podcasters.

♬ original sound – The Wall Street Journal

A story published on October 8 analyzed over 30,000 hours of podcasts and documented how, in recent weeks, right-leaning podcasters had started discussing “affordability” as often as left-leaning podcasters, despite President Trump calling the affordability crisis a “hoax.”

Another story published on October 1 traced anti-AI sentiment, including opposition to Flock surveillance cameras, by analyzing more than four million TikTok videos and thousands of hours of podcasts. The Journal found that posters who shared anti-Flock sentiments disagreed on other political positions about 12% of the time, three times the average rate across other political topics tracked — putting the issue “at the top of the list of positions that unite creators who are otherwise at odds.”

For a story published on October 15, the Journal pulled content about 67 Democratic politicians from its Doppler database. The analysis showed that the Democratic politician currently receiving the most favorable commentary is Angie Nixon, the progressive Senate nominee in Florida. About 70% of TikTok videos posted about her in recent weeks were favorable. She was followed by Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff at 54%. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer ranked the lowest in the analysis; just 3% of videos posted about him were favorable.

Whitaker-Moore said the idea for Doppler was inspired by conversations with Washington bureau chief Damian Paletta and politics editor Christopher Matthews. They thought the coverage of the 2024 U.S. election missed important undercurrents in public opinion that never surfaced in polling. And though reporters acknowledged the power of podcasts in that election cycle, there weren’t many standardized ways to capture what was being said across those channels.

Coming out of those conversations, Whitaker-Moore posed a question to Rob Barry, who leads the Journal’s data journalism team: “Can you build something that can eat the internet and then feed it back to us?”

The Journal had already built its own podcast transcription and summarization tool, Orca. (The name refers to the tight-knit pods in which orcas travel.) Orca had collected countless hours of audio and YouTube videos, not just of political podcasts but from genres like health and wellness.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat can The Wall Street Journal’s new ad campaign tell us about its future?Sarah ScireJune 11, 2024The Journal’s experience with TikTok-based investigations made the social media platform’s videos another natural source of information for Doppler. It’s nearly impossible to create a comprehensive database of TikTok videos, or even a truly random sample. Instead, Barry’s team used a monitoring tool that relies on TikTok’s own recommendation algorithms to identify the accounts it should track.

“Every day we’re adding tons of data across all the different platforms that we’re looking at,” Barry told me. “The database is growing in the background constantly.”

To make sense of that data, Doppler has a tech stack that includes different types of AI models, including LLMs. The model used depends on the specific reporting question.

Embedding models have been central to some of stories published so far. These AI models convert text or images into vectors — lists of numbers that capture the meaning of each piece of content. By vectorizing the content, Doppler can map out the ideas in a dataset and see where they naturally cluster together.

The Journal’s data journalism team has used vectorization in the past, including in its Pulitzer Prize–winning story that mapped out Elon Musk’s entire history of tweets. In Doppler, vectorization facilitates a kind of internet radar, helping reporters identify where patterns are forming across its social media and podcasting database.

For now, the Journal’s political reporters can’t just start using Doppler on their own. The exact methodology has been tailored to each story published, with the help of engineers.

RELATED ARTICLELocal newsrooms are using AI to listen in on public meetingsAndrew DeckMarch 13, 2025“There’s a lot of human judgment in this. My team would not have aimed for a tool that seeks to just produce stuff that we then put directly on the internet,” Barry said. “You still need that human intermediary, that human to apply the judgment and to ask the question.”

The Journal is attaching a short methodology to every story assisted by Doppler. It makes clear that AI was used to produce the piece, briefly explains how the analysis came together, and notes some of the tool’s limitations.

Despite manual spot checks of data classifications and other safeguards to make sure the tool’s outputs are accurate, Barry said, “there’s almost always going to be some level of error and uncertainty and blur around the edges.” The disclosures are one way to “give readers a sense for what that level of issue is.”

Looking ahead, the Journal is considering bringing Doppler to other desks in the newsroom. The data being collected is not inherently political, and it could be used to help answer a host of other reporting questions, drawing on insights scattered across the internet.

“We definitely think that [Doppler News AI] can live beyond the midterms and live beyond elections,” Whitaker-Moore said.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

Improve lead quality by feeding qualification and revenue data back to ad platforms, so automated bidding can prioritize business outcomes over form fills.

This month, a really good question came in:

“My campaigns are generating plenty of leads and hitting our CPA target, but the sales team says the quality is getting worse. How can I optimize for better leads rather than just more conversions?”

The short answer is: If you want better leads, you first need to teach the platform what a better lead looks like.

It’s very easy to lose track of real-world performance when platform-reported performance looks great. Your CPA may be within target and lead volume may look healthy, while your sales team is telling you those leads aren’t turning into meaningful opportunities.

Those two things aren’t necessarily contradictory.

The ad platform may actually be doing exactly what you asked it to do: finding more of the conversions you told it were valuable. If every form fill is treated as the same conversion equally valuable, the bidding system doesn’t inherently know that one became a strong sales opportunity and another went nowhere.

That means improving lead quality starts with the definition of success you’re giving the platform.

In this post, we’ll look at how to define a better outcome, pass that information back to the platform, and give automated bidding enough meaningful signal and time to optimize toward it.

A quick disclosure: I am a Microsoft Advertising employee, and while I’ll reference Microsoft Advertising capabilities where they’re useful, these principles can apply to paid media programs across platforms.

Before changing your bidding strategy or implementing a new measurement tool, ask a more fundamental question:

What actually makes one lead better than another for your business?

For some advertisers, the initial form fill may be meaningful enough. For others, a more granular segmentation might be needed:

The goal should be to get as close as you reasonably can to the deepest meaningful funnel outcome you can reliably measure.

If 100 leads came through but only 10 were SQLs, you don’t want to teach the bidding system that all 100 were equally valuable simply because they completed the same form.

The closer your conversion tracking gets to the outcome the business actually cares about, the more meaningful the information you’re giving the bidding system.

That’s also why marketing and sales alignment matters here. If the platform says CPA is great while Sales says lead quality is deteriorating, both things can be true.

Before optimizing for “better leads,” make sure everyone agrees on what better actually means. Check that your Sales team is using current lead quality to inform their decisions rather than applying historical bias, as lead quality can change and improve over time with campaign optimizations.

See also: The Conversion Setup Errors That Break Smart Bidding

Once you’ve defined the outcome, the next step is giving the platform information that helps distinguish higher-value actions from lower-value ones.

This is where real-world qualification and revenue data become particularly useful. The best signal any ad platform can work off of is conversion values, and passing accurate values will ensure budgets are directed effectively. This is why conversion value rules are so effective: by adapting the conversion value based on probability of value, you can make it even easier for ad platforms to deliver the right leads.

If you aren’t going to use real-world numbers or outcomes, your CPA or ROAS goals may need to be treated as directional guidance rather than representations of actual business results.

There will also be cases where your ultimate outcome doesn’t happen frequently enough to give conversion-based bidding sufficient volume and signal to effectively optimize performance.

That’s where an earlier but still meaningful conversion can help. A lead becoming marketing-qualified, sales-qualified, or progressing further into your funnel tells you more about lead quality than an unrelated engagement metric.

A useful benchmark for automated bidding is at least 30 conversions within 30 days. Following significant changes to budgets or targets, conversion-based bidding can take as many as roughly 50 conversions to calibrate according to multiple platforms.

See also: Ask A PPC: What Are Learning Periods In Digital Marketing?

Once you know which outcomes matter, you need a way to pass that information back to the platform.

If you can’t yet measure true value, identify the most meaningful signal you can track reliably and use conversion value rules to assign it directional value. If you’re able to measure and optimize against real value, use offline conversion imports to bring that data into your ads platform. This can fill in the gaps so platforms optimize against real value.

That’s where mechanisms such as offline conversions and Conversions APIs come in.

Offline conversions let you connect outcomes that happen after the immediate website experience back to the original ad interaction. Think about someone who clicks an ad, fills out a form, talks to a sales contact, and eventually becomes a customer.

Microsoft Advertising, for example, documents the Click ID, conversion time, and conversion goal name among the core information used for offline conversion imports.

And Conversions API, commonly called CAPI, lets conversion information move programmatically from your systems into the ad platform rather than relying exclusively on periodic manual uploads.

Microsoft Advertising’s Conversions API lets advertisers send conversion and engagement events directly from their servers using Universal Event Tracking (UET), and can pass business signals including revenue, product details, click IDs, hashed identifiers, and consent status.

The mechanism isn’t the strategy. The quality of the signal you’re sending through it is.

Before automating the flow of conversion data, make sure you trust the data you’re automating.

If your CRM is treating poor-quality leads as successful outcomes, passing that information back faster won’t solve the problem. You’ll simply create a more efficient feedback loop around the wrong definition of success.

This also applies to gaps in volume or value of conversions. Advertisers should confirm where the gap is appearing:

Auditing for these factors, as much as the technical passing through of conversion data, is a critical step in closing the loop.

See also: Is Your Conversion Data Misleading You? Seven Common Google Ads Tracking Issues

There is one more piece that can easily get overlooked: conversion delay.

Your campaign may look one way when you initially review results and very different after enough time has passed for leads to move through the sales process.

Microsoft Advertising conversion tracking supports configurable conversion windows, depending on the goal, from one minute up to 90 days.

CAPI introduces another consideration. On Microsoft Advertising, CAPI currently has a 90-day look-back window. Consider which outcomes realistically happen soon enough to pass back through that mechanism.

Your systems still need time for sales to work the lead or for a customer to actually convert.

Your reporting cadence should reflect your actual sales cycle, and automated bidding needs enough meaningful data and time to learn.

That may mean resisting the instinct to make aggressive changes because yesterday’s platform numbers don’t yet contain outcomes that take weeks to materialize.

Everything above assumes the campaign’s purpose is ultimately a conversion-driven business outcome.

If you’re running an awareness or consideration campaign, it may generate sales and booked demos, but these should be reported as secondary key performance indicators rather than the appropriate immediate measures of success. Instead of forcing every campaign into the same CPA or ROAS framework, start by being explicit about the business outcome the campaign is intended to drive and select measurement signals appropriate to that objective.

The important thing is consistency between what you want the campaign to accomplish and what you’re asking the platform to optimize toward.

Conversion totals also don’t explain everything happening between an ad interaction and the eventual outcome.

That’s where diagnostic signals can be useful.

Search behavior can help you understand whether you’re creating interest. Search term reporting, for example, can surface changes in branded searches or the kinds of queries coming from your audience.

Microsoft Clarity can help diagnose what happens after the click. Behavioral analytics such as recordings, heatmaps, and engagement insights from your website can help surface whether visitors are meaningfully exploring the site, encountering friction, or leaving without taking the intended action. Clarity AI Visibility can add another discovery signal by showing when content is cited in supported AI-generated experiences and which AI grounding queries triggered those citations.

These signals aren’t substitutes for your business outcome.

Instead, use them to help answer questions the conversion number alone can’t: Are we creating interest? Where are we losing it? Is campaign performance the problem, or is something happening later in the customer journey?

If you want better leads, don’t just ask your ad platform for more conversions. Teach it what a better conversion looks like.

Start by defining the deepest meaningful outcome you can reliably measure. Then pass qualification, revenue, or other value signals back where appropriate, so the platform has a better understanding of what success means to your business.

Use offline conversions, CAPI, or other feedback mechanisms to connect those real-world outcomes with advertising activity. And make sure you’re giving automated bidding enough meaningful signal and enough time to learn from it.

If you choose not to pass those real-world outcomes back, that’s valid too. Just be honest about what your platform metrics represent and keep your internal source of truth at the center of your business decisions.

The platform can only optimize toward the definition of success you give it.

So when lead volume looks great, but quality doesn’t, don’t immediately ask the bidding system to find more.

First, make sure you’ve taught it what “better” means.

Featured Image: Paulo Bobita/Search Engine Journal

#7518. U.K. politicians and German publishers call on regulators to pause Meta’s new terms before October 30 deadline

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The U.K. competition and consumer protection authority sent a formal letter to Meta to discuss its new commercial terms of service.

On Tuesday, Will Hayter, the executive director for digital markets at the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA), shared the update during a session of the communications and digital committee of British Parliament, after a member of the House of Lords pressed him about Meta’s new terms. Hayter said he scheduled a meeting with the tech giant today to seek clarity on the new terms, though the CMA declined to provide any further details.

RELATED ARTICLELegal experts warn Meta’s new terms still grant broad scraping permissions, despite language changesAndrew DeckOctober 17, 2026Last week, Nieman Lab broke the news that the terms would permit mass scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts on Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads. The new terms are slated to take effect on October 30, and there is currently no option to opt out. Virtually every news organization owns at least one Meta business account.

“Are you going to pause the deadline? I mean, [it’s in] a week,” Veronica Wadley, Baroness Fleet and a former editor of the Evening Standard, said during the session of Parliament. “You know this includes almost every U.K. news publisher and it is clearly uncompetitive leverage of Meta’s strategic market position.”

In the same session, Sarah Cardell, the CEO of CMA, said the authority had limited intervention options because it has not formally designated Meta as an “entrenched market power” (something it has done in the past for Google and Apple). Cardell said other competition enforcement actions are a possibility, but the CMA is “urgently” seeking more information from Meta before making any judgment.

Over the weekend, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” But legal experts told Nieman Lab the revised terms would still permit mass scraping.

A Meta spokesperson said on Saturday that the company revised the language because it “wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.”

Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of service.

“Does Meta think we can’t read?” Theo Bamber, chief executive of the U.K.’s News Media Association, wrote in a LinkedIn post on Monday. “We know you’ve taken the word ‘train’ out but changing it to ‘develop’ isn’t fooling anyone.”

News publisher associations across Europe have called on regulators to intervene before the terms take effect next week.

On Tuesday, two major German publisher associations called on the European Commission to prohibit the new terms from going into effect until a complete review had been conducted. Together, the German Association of Free Press and the Federal Association of Digital Publishers represent more than 9,000 media brands across Europe.

RELATED ARTICLEMeet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAIAndrew DeckFebruary 20, 2025“Meta intends to automatically capture, copy, and store the complete websites and archives of publishers and analyze them for its own automated and non-automated commercial products,” reads a joint statement from the associations. “This makes access to Meta’s platforms contingent on the free surrender of the entire digital publishing product. This is blatant theft.”

The statement alleges that Meta’s new terms could be in violation of the E.U. Digital Markets Act, which was passed in 2022 to curb the dominance of big tech companies and create fairer competition across the region. The publishers cited a specific clause that guarantees “fair, reasonable, and non-discriminatory general conditions of access for business users.”

The uproar from European publishers echoes similar opposition to the new terms from major U.S. publisher associations. Jason Kint, the CEO of Digital Content Next, has been vocal about his skepticism of the new terms since Nieman Lab’s story broke last week.

“Meta’s supposed Friday night correction to its new commercial terms is a farce,” he wrote in a statement published on Tuesday. “Exactly what you’d expect from a gatekeeper notorious for abusing its market power.”

ISO (the name stands for “in search of”) is a wide-reaching management firm that touch categories like beauty, food, and art, but its roots are deepest in the gaming and streamer communities. Influence Media Partners is backing ISO as the new firm takes shape. “The next household name is already online, building an audience, and ISO was built for that talent. Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

New holiday data counts ads inside Google AI Overviews, AI Mode and ChatGPT across five shopping categories and shows which prompts ChatGPT ads ran on.

Adthena reported that approximately 175,100 paid ad placements were found within Google’s AI Overview panel as well as AI Mode panels inside the U.S. during the period of June to September. This included five holiday shopping categories; however, the majority of these paid placements belonged to apparel and consumer electronics.

The Holiday AI Paid Search Report also counts 204,489 ChatGPT ad placements in the same five categories over the same months. Adthena sells ad tracking for Google and ChatGPT, and the report closes with an offer for a free trial of its ChatGPT Ads product.

Some U.S. apparel and electronics advertisers may already be using portions of their existing campaigns to serve ads to users who see AI Overviews and AI Mode. The report identifies where the ads appeared, but does not track which ads were clicked, how much was spent, nor what conversions were achieved on either surface.

The total number of ads in Google’s AI Answers (in the U.S.) in this report is based upon a combined total for both AI Overviews and AI Mode. In that count, apparel has approximately 111,000 placements; consumer electronics have about 55,000; travel has roughly 6,500; beauty has about 2,100; and toys and games have around 685.

There are no separate ad buys for these placement types. According to Google’s Help Page regarding Ads in AI-Powered Experiences, all Search, Shopping, and Performance Max campaigns that exist are automatically eligible to appear in AI-Answers. Although advertisers cannot specifically target only AI Overviews or AI Mode, or opt out of those placements apart from Search, they may still utilize negative keyword targeting and/or brand exclusions.

The report also reviewed how many times AI Overviews appeared in Google Results for both August of 2025 and August of 2026. Going from 304 million to 575 million, U.S. appearances saw an 89% increase over that period. The UK/EU saw an increase of 160%, while Australia saw an increase of 536%. The report doesn’t describe the queries behind those counts or say whether the set stayed the same across both years.

The report counts 204,489 ChatGPT Ads placements across five categories, Apparel, Consumer Electronics, Travel, Toys & Games and Beauty, from June through September 2026.

Adthena’s press release frames it more broadly, stating more than 200,000 advertisement placements occurred since OpenAI started allowing others to buy advertising space on the chatbot.

In the report’s count, apparel accounted for the largest number of advertisement placements at 90,517. Next was Consumer Electronics with 56,569; then Travel with 48,134; followed by Toys and Games with 4,694 and lastly Beauty with 4,575.

In addition, the company reported that there were 1,082 different advertisers in those five categories using the service in June, 3,741 advertisers in July, and 6,333 advertisers in August. The company projected the number of advertisers in September.

According to the report, the advertisers in its data in Toys and Games increased the most during that time frame from June to August, increasing 13 fold, from what the company calls a relatively low base.

The report states that the total number of advertiser placements included in their research covered all markets, but does not identify which markets or state whether they continued to monitor the same market(s)/queries throughout the entire four-month period. In addition, OpenAI expanded its footprint during that time.

On August 18, OpenAI announced that ChatGPT Ads would be available in 31 European countries. The company began offering this service one week later. Additionally, on September 23, OpenAI began rolling out ChatGPT Ads to seven additional Asian markets.

For perspective, on October 21 OpenAI stated that more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT Ads since the advertising capability was opened up to outside parties just over eight months earlier. This figure represents all categories and the complete period of time that ChatGPT Ads has been open to third-party advertisers, so it isn’t directly comparable to the report’s monthly counts.

In addition to that, the report groups ChatGPT ads based on the nature of the search that an ad was run against. It describes research and discovery queries as “people comparing or asking what’s best rather than naming a product.”

In beauty, 83% of ads ran on those queries, while travel and toys & games were at 69% and 67% respectively. Apparel and consumer electronics came in under half, at 48% and 42% respectively.

Again, the press release references only the data related to beauty, travel and toys. The report provides no information about how questions were categorized.

Since Google includes searches that prompt ads in AI Overviews and AI Mode in aggregate in its standard reports for all of Search, they are intermingled throughout your search terms report.

In ChatGPT, best-of and comparison prompts carried most of the observed ads in beauty, travel & toys, and less than 50% of those seen in apparel and electronics.

After the report’s time frame closed, Google’s ads within their AI answers continued to evolve. Google announced that they were launching multi-turn ads in the United States on October 28. These allow advertisers’ ads to show up on subsequent searches (queries) in AI Mode. In addition, Google stated that ads in AI Mode are scaling to ten additional countries including Canada and Australia. They further stated that Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom were planned for Q4 2026.

OpenAI’s October 21 announcement expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries. The most recent Adthena data is from September so does not include these new developments nor the weeks surrounding Black Friday.

#7515. In the AI age, publishers who understand what readers want will do best, a new report argues

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

AI inverts the traditional journalism hierarchy: Instead of reporters gathering information, editors deciding how to present it, and newsrooms releasing the same final story to everyone, AI agents deliver what readers ask for, refining or expanding on information as requested.

It’s “an interactive process in a way the current news system isn’t,” write the authors of “The Three-Layer Cake: Public-Interest Information in an AI-Intermediated Age,” released Wednesday by the Tow-Knight Center for Journalism Futures at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY. (The cake’s three layers are “the products that identify what people want to know, the systems that synthesize answers, and the organizations that produce the underlying reporting.”)

Some interesting ideas from the report by Gina Chua and Adiel Kaplan:

This new age may be better for some readers. The authors write:

There are people the old system never reached, or never reached well. A parent who hears of school budget cuts may want to know if their child’s elementary school art class will survive. No newsroom would assign that story. It matters to a handful of families whose children attend a single school, and the exact answer is uncertain. A well-designed AI system could pull together what is known from reporting and context and offer a nuanced response — fulfilling an information need that previously did not have enough economic power to be met directly.

Similarly, minority communities whose concerns didn’t rise to the level of interest of a city newspaper might have rarely seen their perspectives reflected in coverage in the past. Coverage in the mainstream media of the AIDS epidemic in the early 1980s was often focused on the risk to the heterosexual population rather than on the gay community it ravaged. An AI system that can access information from and about underserved communities could rectify that.

Publishers opting out could make the information environment worse. If news organizations seek to prevent AI from using their content, they may contribute to a poorer “information commons,” the authors argue. It “works as a strategy for individual organizations, but cedes the broader mission of providing information to the vast majority of the public to others who may not have the public’s interests at heart.”

Scoops and exclusives are a “luxury” — and they’re losing value fast.

Even a pivot to investigative reporting, as important a public good as that is, is not necessarily a solution. Much of investigative journalism is summarizable once it is published, even if the original story breaks important news and is a delight to read. As Francesco Marconi noted, a multi-month investigation could cost a newsroom $200,000 in resources, then drop in economic value to close to zero within minutes of publication. Both investigations and scoops can have huge social value and help build a brand, but economically, they provide little lasting value to their newsrooms — and even less so in an AI-intermediated landscape. “Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write: In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference. The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

“Commoditized news” isn’t saving anyone. Publishers have to make “hard choices” about what they’ll cover, the authors write:

In an AI-intermediated world, commoditized news carries little value, especially if it’s already available in some other form. That’s not to say that day-to-day coverage of municipal government, a core task of many local newsrooms, should go away; only that its coverage needs to be differentiated from what could be found elsewhere or summarized from a meeting transcript, for it to hold value. Differentiation might involve adding context to the coverage through original reporting, or asking questions that wouldn’t otherwise be asked at a press conference.

The deeper and more specialized a newsroom’s area of coverage and expertise is, the less likely it is to be duplicated by other organizations — and that provides both pricing power and closer links to the communities that value such information.

#7514. Have you heard? Ethan and Hila’s divorce, Harvard’s creator summit, and Brandon Herrera’s defeat.

Each week, we handpick a selection of stories to give you a snapshot of trends, updates, business moves, and more from around the creator industry.

This week, infidelity is bringing an end to a high-profile creator marriage, the Ivy League is hosting a new kind of summit, and we’re still waiting for the first creator in Congress.

Hila Klein files for divorce as Ethan’s affair becomes public. The Kleins were well known as co-hosts of a podcast and YouTube channel, but Ethan is being removed from his positions after his indiscretions came to light. And that’s not all — Hila wasted no time filing for divorce. She had already made that decision before the news became public, and she will seek joint custody of the couple’s kids while also restoring her maiden name.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Sour Patch Kids owner sues Ryan Trahan over candy brand Joyride. Consumer goods giant Mondelez is arguing that Trahan’s candies were designed to be confused with Sour Patch Kids, because they’re human-shaped and wrapped in colorful packaging. The actual case might be complicated, but this is yet another roadblock for a creator-led consumable product.

Alex Cooper heads to CAA after UTA exit. The Call Her Daddy host will look to turn over a new leaf as she brings a new talent firm into her corner. CAA is choosing to represent Cooper, her husband Matt Kaplan, and their media company Unwell, so the L.A.-based agency is making a big bet on a major Gen Z tastemaker.

Harvard University’s School of Public Health hosted a creator summit. More than a dozen creators were in attendance as Harvard looked to improve the quality of health information of social media. Platforms like TikTok are increasingly popular as sources of medical advice for Gen Z users, so the summit is an important step in the right direction as healthcare professionals look to counteract the spread of misinformation.

YouTube is bringing a Grand Theft Auto “creator collective” to London. On October 17, two days before the arrival of the much-anticipated next chapter in Rockstar Games’ open world franchise, YouTube will gather gamers and creators in West London for an event that will celebrate the launch of GTA VI. The game is expected to be the biggest gaming tentpole of the year, so it’s no surprise to see platforms pulling out all the stops to generate excitement.

Can Paris Creator Week become the Cannes of the creator economy? That question was on everyone’s mind as 8,000 attendees flocked to the French capital for two days of typical convention fare. All of the major social media players were represented, as were European content producers like Banijay. All of a sudden, France has become a major hotbed for creator events.

Firearms YouTuber Brandon Herrera lost his Congressional bid. Running for a House seat in a deep-red district, Herrera was favored to become the first Congressman whose career began on social media. But the blue wave that crashed down in Texas swept Herrera aside, as Democrat Katy Padilla Stout earned a comfortable victory that will send Herrera back to YouTube.

TikTok edits might not be the right choice for political ads. That was one takeaway from a recent study that examined the social media messaging of Kamala Harris’ 2024 presidential run. The researchers concluded that traditional ads work better on social media than posts that try to adopt those platforms’ stylistic conventions. Translation: Promote your campaign on TikTok, but keep it simple, stupid.

Jubilee follows up election stream with short-form push. The media company delivered its first election special on the night of the 2026 midterms, and days later, it announced its first two short-form originals. Dateable and People Spotting will help Jubilee break into new territory as it builds on its reputation as a wide-reaching content producer aimed at Gen Z.

The financials of Instagram’s move into long-form content are drawing questions. Creators want to buy into Instagram’s plan for 90-minute videos, but without a robust revenue stream attached, some are skeptical. “Exposure as a form of payment and with the intention of cutting into YouTube’s market share and cutting into the amount of views people are getting on YouTube — it’s just gross,” digital strategist and creator Gabriella Zutrau told Digiday. “Instagram has never valued creators.”

YouTube’s app redesign has proven to be perplexing. The new version of the YouTube app moves the Subscriptions tab to a menu that goes away once the user starts scrolling through their feed. YouTube redesigns are always unpopular at first, but the platform’s repeated minimizations of its famous subscriptions is definitely a curious choice.

Snapchat’s subscription offerings now have 30 million customers. As Snap Inc. revealed its earnings for the third quarter of 2026, it touted the continued success of products like Snapchat+ and Lens+. By offering premium features in exchange for a cost-effective monthly price, subscriptions have become a key part of Snap’s business model and monetization suite.

Why watch YouTube when you can build your own in two hours. That’s what Andrej Karpathy did with a little help from a fellow named Claude. The result of that effort is HackerTube, which contains thousands of videos related to the titular subject and shows what can be accomplished with AI-assisted coding.

Why is ‘Sacrifice’ the first Elton John music video with one billion YouTube views? ‘Sacrifice’ is a 1989 single that peaked at #18 on the charts, but it gave John his first entry in the Billion Views Club. You would think that ‘Tiny Dancer,’ ‘Your Song,’ or ‘Benny and the Jets’ would have broken through first, but it’s going to be a long, long time before those singles can match ‘Sacrifice’ on YouTube.

Humanoid robots put to work at a China supermarket are “slacking off.” Why bust your circuits when you can just quiet quit like all those humans who programmed you? The bots’ questionable work ethic is just smart — that’s why they call it artificial intelligence.

#7511. The Ringer bets on Substack’s network over its own website

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

Once synonymous with independent writers, Substack is increasingly home to established publishers.

“Very interesting that The Ringer’s writers write on Substack and not…The Ringer.” “What’s the point of the website then?” “Hold up. You’re telling me The Ringer would rather make money on writing than not make money on writing?”

These were some of the responses after The Ringer’s Zach Lowe announced his new newsletter. The Lowe Post, which covers the NBA, joins The Ringer’s Sean Fennessey, Tom Pelissero, and Bryan Curtis on Substack. (The Lowe Post is $10 a month, and has already become one of Substack’s bestselling sports newsletters. Fennessey’s newsletter is $5 a month; Pelissero’s is $8 a month, and Curtis’s is free.)

Though podcasting has been his main gig for a while now, Zach Lowe is one of the best sports writers in the country — witty, warm-hearted, and a true lover of basketball and the Mets. In his inaugural newsletter, he wrote about how he feels his sports analysis loses a step when he’s only talking, not writing.

On the one hand, of course Lowe should have a newsletter. But his Substack, and those of his colleagues, are not independent side hustles. Each has Spotify and The Ringer branding.

As a digital media business, The Ringer has always been flexible and opportunistic. It was initially published on Medium when it launched in 2016. The publication moved to an ad and tech partnership with Vox in 2017. It was acquired by Spotify for $250 million in 2020 and, five years later, signed a distribution deal with Netflix to bring some of its video podcasts (including The Bill Simmons Show, The Zach Lowe Show, and The Rewatchables) to the platform. The website has always been free to read.

The Ringer declined to comment on its Substack strategy and would not tell me whether the writers receive a share of subscription revenue. (The lack of comment has garnered its own press coverage.) Though The Ringer has referred to the new newsletters as being in “partnership” with Substack, there’s no separate financial relationship between the two companies, Substack confirmed.

If you find this a little strange, you’re not wrong. The Substack-Ringer whatever-this-is is a confusing move that is raising a lot of very 2026 questions. Here are some things I’m wondering.

While Grantland — the beloved sports writing site created by Ringer founder Bill Simmons in 2011 and shuttered by ESPN in 2015 — was known for its long-form journalism, The Ringer is all-in on podcasts. Simmons jokes on nearly every episode of his own show that his “fingers stopped working” years ago and that his days writing columns are behind him.

Today, most of the links on The Ringer’s homepage will bring you somewhere else. The homepage’s function is closer to a landing page or linktree than a news website. Many links redirect to Spotify, where listeners can watch or listen to Ringer podcasts. Now, with the newsletter launches, several links whisk you off The Ringer and over to Substack.

Burned by Facebook and forever-shifting algorithmic winds, many publishers have focused on building on their own channels in recent years. The theory is that direct-to-reader news products like newsletters, apps, and events will help publishers control audience connections and insulate them from inevitable platform pivots.

But though Substack was once synonymous with independent writers, its perks are luring more and more established publications onto the platform. Some, like The Ringer, are sharing Substack-exclusive content. Others, like New York magazine and The Wall Street Journal, are redistributing work that exists elsewhere on the internet.

One major pull? Substack has morphed into a full-on social media platform, albeit one where publishers can directly monetize and capture email addresses for themselves.

In the past six months, the app has generated nearly 800,000 paid subscriptions, according to Substack, and more than half of those subscriptions came directly from its Twitter-like Notes feed. Network effects account for more than half of all subscriptions on the platform and about 30% of paid subscriptions, a spokesperson said.

Media journalist Simon Owens has been tracking the rise of traditional media outlets on Substack (on Substack, naturally).

“Open web” is an ill-defined concept. Sometimes people use it to mean the public portion of the internet that’s indexable by search engines. Others mean, basically, websites — anything you can reach on a web browser at a URL. Whatever the semantics, people have been shoveling dirt on “the open web” for years. (This New York Times obituary noting the rise of paywalls, apps, and tiers of access was published back in 2010.) But the death notices have picked up with the rise of AI.

RELATED ARTICLESearch traffic has declined so much that some publishers are considering opting out of Google entirelyNeel DhaneshaJuly 22, 2026Google Search referrals to publisher websites are down 40.2% year over year, according to Chartbeat. And AI chatbots are not sending users to news sites. Referrals from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, and the like were just 0.01% of traffic to publishers and declining, Chartbeat found.

Even before it was acquired by Spotify, The Ringer’s primary business was podcasts, so it’s never been as reliant on search as text-first publishers. The Ringer can afford to deprioritize its website more than most. But all kinds of publishers are having to respond to a real shift in the way people consume news and content.

RELATED ARTICLEWhat’s it take to make a great daily newsletter? Axios’ Kendall Baker is planning to bring one to Yahoo SportsJoshua BentonAugust 17, 2023Kendall Baker, senior writer and head of newsletters for Yahoo Sports, knows a thing or two about email newsletters. He says The Ringer’s move exemplifies a news consumption trend that’s only picking up speed.

“Most people’s general way of finding information or consuming information online is that they’re opening their phone and going straight to a social media app and starting to scroll,” Baker said.

Another app that most U.S. adults open up every day? Their email.

“If I want an engaged audience on a daily basis, relying on them coming to find me versus going to them would be silly — and it’s becoming more and more silly,” he said. “I think that’s partially what’s driving this. Newsletters are an obvious solution there.”

The Ringer’s move is also a bet on the strength of individual personalities. Substack doesn’t (yet) offer bundles, so a reader who wants all of The Ringer’s paid Substack content will have to fork over something like $23/month — more than a subscription to New York magazine or Apple News and a little less than a full New York Times bundle. Even with the strong parasocial relationships The Ringer enjoys — enough to fuel many, many subreddits — the pricing was a common complaint online.

Many publishers will not want to cannibalize pricier subscriptions by selling access to a single popular writer. Offering a whole-site subscription also lets readers discover (and hopefully fall in love with!) more of your content.

“It seems in the Substack era, you’re writing for people who really like you,” Simmons said on a recent podcast about sportswriting. “And you’re getting that audience but then, how do you pull other people in? That’s going to be the big question over the next five to 10 years.”

“Obviously we have a lot of writing on The Ringer dot com that we’re very proud of,” Simmons added, pointing to a NFL Take-O-Meter piece by The Ringer’s Austin Gayle. “But will it ever be like 2011 again? I don’t know.”

“You mean, when we launched Grantland?” The Ringer’s Bryan Curtis asked.

“No, just that era. How many writers were coming up — the energy behind it, and all the different styles,” Simmons said. “I wonder if we’ll ever have that many writers again trying that many different things.”

#7510. Just a quarter of U.S. adults trust creators to always disclose brand deals

Just one in four U.S. adults believe content creators consistently disclose brand ties when promoting a sponsored product.

That’s not a lot of trust for an industry that relies on creators building close bonds with their audiences.

The data comes from a Morning Consult survey conducted for Business Insider; around 2,000 people participated.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, older folks were less inclined to trust creators: 53% of Baby Boomers said creators “rarely or never” clearly disclose paid deals, while just 21% of Gen Z said the same thing.

Morning Consult also asked respondents whether creators should have to disclose paid sponsorships at all. Across all age groups, the majority of people said yes.

But some did say no: 12% of Boomers, 18% of Gen Xers, 22% of Millennials, and 23% of Gen Z’ers.

We find this wild, and if you’ll forgive a second of conjecture, we’re wondering if the striking number of nos among Millennials and Gen Z has to do with people in those generations being raised in a culture of online side hustles and low barriers to content creation. How many of these respondents are creators themselves, or wish they were, or think they could be, if they just started making TikTok Shop promo videos like their friends and coworkers?

To them, it might seem like a drag to make a video hoping to earn a quick buck, only to have to admit “Yeah, I’m selling something,” in an obvious place.

It seems that way to some established creators and brands, too. BI also cited a recent survey from SheSpeaks where 14% of creators admitted they don’t always disclose brand ties, and 18% said that within the past year, a brand had explicitly asked them not to disclose that they had been paid.

If you’re a regular Tubefilter reader, you will of course know that behavior is very against Federal Trade Commission regulations, and could open violative creators and businesses up to hefty fines. There is never an excuse for an individual creator failing to disclose, but a business that makes it standard to push creators not to disclose is even more problematic.

And while disclosures might seem like a drag to these creators and businesses, to most other people, transparency is reassuring.

Emily Steele, CEO of creator marketing platform Hummingbirds, told BI another key aspect here is that creators need to have meaningful and engaging content outside of brand deals for their audiences to be open when they endorse a product.

“There are creators who only post UGC or sponsored content without any cohesion around what they’re posting about and why,” she said. “Why would I, as a follower, trust you when I feel like all you post is a paid brand deal?”
