#7436. TikTok launches standalone shopping app

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The new platform is focused on product discovery and purchasing but is currently only available to a handful of countries in Asia.

TikTok is trying to lure shoppers with a dedicated TikTok Shop app now available for download in select markets in Asia.

As shown in these example screens, the TikTok Shop app is focused primarily on product listings and driving shopping behavior, although some TikTok video content is also accessible.

Alongside personalized product suggestions inspired by user interests, the app also offers select livestreams and short videos to add context to certain product listings.

As explained by TikTok: “Discover trending finds, exclusive deals and shopping support you can count on — all in one place.”

It’s TikTok’s latest effort to enhance shopping behavior, and get more people viewing its platform as a place for product discovery.

That’s been central to the company’s expanded success in China, where the local version of the app, called Douyin, now generates a significant amount of income from in-app sales.

According to KrAsia, Douyin generated nearly $500 billion in gross merchandise volume in 2025, with livestream commerce in particular, driving a significant portion of that activity.

TikTok has been trying to push shopping in its app as well in order to replicate the expanded revenue potential that Douyin has seen from integrating shopping into the video viewing experience.

This play has driven some success, though not on the same scale as in China.

According to Marketing Maze, TikTok globally generated $26.2 billion GMV in the first half of 2025.

Part of the challenge appears to be that TikTok users are seemingly less interested in shopping in-stream, preferring instead to visit separate apps. Shoppers in the U.S., for example, seem more habitually aligned to shopping on Amazon, while they watch videos on TikTok or YouTube. Virtually every social app has tried to merge the two, but none have succeeded in driving significant shopping activity.

Maybe the addition of a separate shopping app could better align with this behavior while still keeping shoppers within the TikTok ecosystem. That could also help to better associate TikTok’s brand with shopping activity and ultimately benefit its broader shopping push.

As reported by social media expert Matt Navarra, the TikTok Shop app is currently available in Singapore, Thailand, Malaysia and the Philippines.

Supabase manages millions of Postgres instances and is growing. We have strong teams across observability, release engineering, and incident management — and we're concentrating our reliability efforts into a dedicated SRE practice that ties the discipline together across the platform.

You'll be embedded within Service Operations, and your primary job is to make every engineering team more reliable — not by owning their infrastructure, but by establishing the practices, frameworks, and feedback loops that let them own reliability themselves. You'll work across the org: sometimes setting the standard, sometimes pair-programming a fix, sometimes helping a team define their error budget, sometimes telling them it's exhausted.

This role is ideal for someone who has a strong vision for how SRE should work and thrives in async, fast-paced environments where influence matters more than authority.

Partner with service teams to define meaningful SLIs and SLOs grounded in customer experience, and build the error budget policies that turn them into engineering decisions

Own and evolve the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process — conducting reviews for new services and major changes across observability, alerting, runbooks, capacity, and graceful degradation

Strengthen the incident-to-improvement pipeline: connecting postmortem findings to operational readiness gaps, identifying repeat failure patterns, and driving systemic fixes

Act as the reliability expert teams pull in for architecture reviews, failure mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design

Identify and quantify operational toil across the org, and build or advocate for automation that eliminates it

Help teams design sustainable on-call practices: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction

Track and report on org-wide operational maturity, surfacing systemic gaps and driving remediation

Have 7+ years of experience in SRE, production engineering, or reliability-focused roles, including experience shaping SRE practices and driving adoption across engineering teams

Have a software engineering mindset — you write code and build tools, not just configure them

Have hands-on experience defining and operationalizing SLOs/SLIs at scale, including error budget policies that actually influenced engineering decisions

Have deep experience with incident response, postmortem facilitation, and turning incident learnings into systemic improvements

Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems (bonus: managed database platforms or Postgres)

Are proficient with cloud infrastructure (AWS preferred) and infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred, Terraform/CDK also acceptable)

Communicate clearly and persuasively — this role requires influencing without authority across a distributed org

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by making other teams more effective rather than being the one who fixes everything

Experience with Kubernetes-based platform operations

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling

Experience building developer-facing reliability tooling (SLO dashboards, ORR frameworks, toil tracking, DORA metrics)

#7433. Meta, TikTok and Google push back on California law

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The companies are arguing that a new law set to take effect next year violates First Amendment rights and oversteps regulatory boundaries, per Reuters.

Social media giants Meta and TikTok have got another major legal fight on their hands as they join Google in seeking to block the enforcement of a new law in California that would force them to stop using “psychologically exploitative features” on users under age 16.

California’s Assembly Bill 1709, which was signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom on Sept. 10, says that online platforms operating in the state are required to restrict the usage of certain addictive features for users under age 16.

Per the text of the law, those addictive elements include “addictive feeds, endless scrolls, autoplay, and their functional equivalents, including any feature that learns from user information or behavior in order to prolong engagement with a particular internet website, online service, online application, or mobile application.”

Under this new law, social platforms are essentially required to either remove these elements from the accounts of underage users, or ban users under age 16 from using their platforms. The law is currently scheduled to come into effect on Jan. 1.

But as reported by Reuters, platforms are pushing back on these restrictions and arguing that they violate the First Amendment, as well as Section 230 protections for online providers.

As per Reuters: “In separate lawsuits on Wednesday, Google, Meta and TikTok ​said the law wrongly compels them to honor the state’s preferred means of presenting ⁠content to children, and substitutes the state’s judgment for that of parents.”

The argument these platforms are making is that California legislators are overstepping regulatory boundaries in order to impose restrictive operating conditions that infringe on users’ rights.

It’s the latest in a series of significant legal challenges relating to potential teen harm facing social media platforms.

In March, a jury in California found that apps including Facebook, Instagram and YouTube can have significant mental health impacts, particularly on younger users, due to intentionally designed, addictive systems. The jury ruled that both Meta and YouTube parent company Alphabet ignored these risks in order to maximize business opportunities.

Then in August, as part of a separate case, Meta agreed to pay more than $18 billion to halt a potentially damaging lawsuit over social media harms. As part of that settlement, Meta also agreed to implement new restrictions on teen social media use.

These cases have led to the implementation of California’s new law, which the platforms are now seeking to push back on in order to limit the impact of these findings.

Social platforms are also facing various new laws that would ban teens from using their apps entirely in many regions.

#7432. The New Organic Growth Stack: Search, Social, Communities & AI

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

AI search now runs on two internets. Build the organic stack that gets your brand cited on both, prioritizing pages, communities, video & reviews.

Your rankings are holding. Your clicks aren’t.

Google’s AI features answer the question on the results page, and the searcher never leaves. From January to April 2026, 68% of U.S. Google searches ended without a click. And less of Google’s traffic reaches the open web than it used to.

Because for a growing share of B2B buyers, the search doesn’t start on Google at all. It starts in an AI chatbot.

Google’s results page, its AI features, and the standalone LLMs all pull from a mix of sources. Reddit threads. YouTube videos. Review profiles. LinkedIn posts. Comparison pages.

That’s your organic growth stack. It’s also the mix your buyers use to build a shortlist.

If you only optimize your site, you’re competing for a shrinking slice of the pool. To stay competitive, SEO has to expand beyond on-site.

Today, I’ll show you which sources each surface leans on and what to build first.

For our State of B2B AI Discovery 2026 report with AirOps, we tracked roughly 380,000 AI answers covering 81 enterprise software topics across six AI surfaces. Unless linked otherwise, the figures below come from this study.

Let’s start with what didn’t change. Product pages still get cited more than anything else.

Across every AI surface we tracked, vendor sites, integrators, and tool directories took the largest share of citations. That ranged from 52% on Perplexity to 72% on Gemini. Review sites added another 9% to 21%.

Remember: Vendor share isn’t yours by default. It includes your competitors’ sites and the software directories that list you side-by-side.

This is the stack’s foundation, and it’s crowded. Your product pages compete with your rivals’ pages. The comparison pages written about you compete with the ones you write yourself.

The layers above the foundation are where search starts to splinter.

Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode ground their answers in live Google Search results. They inherit what already ranks. ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Perplexity run their own retrieval.

The citations split right along that line.

Google’s two AI surfaces put 7% of their citations into social platforms like YouTube and LinkedIn. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude sit at 0.3% or below.

So “AI visibility” is at least two games.

A brand can be everywhere in Google’s AI answers but invisible in ChatGPT and the other standalone models. Or the reverse. Using a blended visibility score hides each one’s contribution.

See also: Wikipedia, Podcasts & Reddit Now Drive AI Citations, Ask Your PR Team How They Did It

Organic visibility now comes down to surface coverage: showing up on the domains each AI surface trusts most.

Your new organic growth stack has to address both internets. Here’s how to do it.

See also: What Search Engines Trust Now: Authority, Freshness & First-Party Signals

AI tools are catching on fast with B2B buyers. According to G2, 51% of B2B software buyers now start their research in an AI chatbot more often than Google, up from 29% a year earlier.

But Google still dominates search overall. It handles roughly three-quarters of all desktop searches. AI Overviews alone reach 2.5 billion monthly users and another billion use AI Mode.

I still think ranking matters. It just doesn’t guarantee a citation anymore. AI Overviews have been pulling fewer citations from top-ranking pages.

The standalone engines lean on product pages too.

Gemini sends 72% of its citations to vendor and product domains, while G2 shows up in just 14% of its answers. Gemini is choosing between vendor pages, and yours are up against everyone else’s in your category.

Eighty-four of the 100 most-cited URLs in our data were either comparison pages (59) or listicles (25). Together, they drew over 66,000 citations. Whoever writes those pages shapes how AI frames your category.

A lot of teams pour budget into the blog and let product and comparison pages go stale. I’d flip that. Fix the pages AI already cites before you write another post.

As James Scherer, Foundation’s VP of Strategy, puts it: “Editorial gets the budget; product pages get the citations.”

Action: Identify the 10 most-cited comparison pages and listicles in your category. Check how you’re framed in each one. Then publish your own comparison page against your top three competitors.

Reddit was the most-cited external domain in our dataset, earning 159,000 citations across 12,500 unique URLs.

Reddit’s logged-out users, who mostly arrive from search engines, grew 27% year over year in Q2 2026. They now outnumber logged-in users, 77.7 million to 52.6 million. Threads rank on Google. Google sends readers into the threads. Then Google’s AI features cite them.

But those layers can also shift fast. After reports that ChatGPT was citing Reddit less, we extended our tracking and found its Reddit citation rate fell from 21% in July to 10% in August, while Google’s surfaces kept citing Reddit.

How much community platforms like Reddit matter also depends on your category. Community citations ranged from 5% of the total for SEO platforms to 14% for EDR/XDR security tools.

If you’re new to the platform, start with this SEJ AMA with a Reddit marketing veteran.

My biggest advice: Don’t treat Reddit like a launch channel. I’d trade one viral thread for steady, useful answers across 50.

Action: Spread your effort across many threads and subreddits. Don’t bet on one. Track community citations weekly, because monthly reporting would have missed a drop like ChatGPT’s.

LinkedIn is a Google-surface play. It reaches 13% of AI Mode answers, 9% of AI Overviews, and 6% of Perplexity’s. ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude didn’t cite it at all.

Across B2B software categories, social is the second-largest citation source after brand and product content, at 6%.

LinkedIn is where executives and practitioners set the category narrative. Google’s AI features pick up that narrative. It’s why employee amplification belongs in the stack.

Don’t fall into the likes and follows trap. If the goal is getting cited, watch whether Google’s AI answers pick up the way your people describe the category.

Action: Pick the category questions you want to own. Post on them every week from executives and practitioners. Measure the impact in AI Overviews and AI Mode, since that’s where LinkedIn gets cited.

YouTube shows up in 47% of AI Mode’s citing answers and 38% of AI Overviews.

It’s tempting to read that as Google favoring its own property, but our data complicates that. Gemini is also a Google product, and yet YouTube showed up in 0.3% of its citations: roughly 17x less than on AI Overviews.

The difference is how each surface finds its sources. AI Overviews and AI Mode are Search features. Google uses query fan-out, running multiple related searches to build each answer, so videos that already rank in Search get pulled in.

A lot of B2B videos are made for people who already know your brand and product. But the videos that earn a place in this layer answer the questions buyers ask before they’ve picked a vendor.

Action: Ship comparison, alternatives, and best-of videos. Title them the way your buyers phrase the question.

The standalone engines lean hard on review sites. Claude and Perplexity draw about one in five citations from review domains.

Claude’s third-party citations are almost entirely review platforms. G2 appears in 30% of the Claude answers that cite sources. Capterra appears in 13%, and Gartner and PeerSpot in about 9% each.

Category matters here too. Review citations ranged from 8% in managed databases to 25% in ATS and recruiting software.

Buyers back this up. In G2’s 2026 research, review sites (38%) narrowly passed AI chatbots (37%) as the top source shaping B2B software shortlists.

G2 isn’t a one-time push. For Claude and Perplexity, your profile is a live source, so run it like one.

Action: Give your G2 profile a named owner and a monthly review target.

Nobody builds every layer at once. Run two checks before you start.

Copy the wrong organic growth stack, and you end up investing in the wrong channels. The AirOps data shows just how much the source mix changes from industry to industry, even within the SaaS space.

The managed database niche is an illustrative example. A brand in this space that borrows an HR tech playbook pours budget into review sites, which earn just 8% of that category’s citations. Meanwhile, it starves communities, which earn 13%.

Once you know which layers matter in your category, match them to the team you have. At every size, the question is the same: which internet are you still missing?

Run a fixed set of 100+ prompts on a schedule. Track citation rate and share for each AI surface. Set an alert for any 20% week-over-week swing.

Watch sentiment per platform, too. On the same prompts, AirOps’ 100-point sentiment scores ranged from 81 on Perplexity to 69 on Claude.

Then tie it back to the numbers leadership already watches, like branded searches, referral traffic, and pipeline sourced from your content.

The first quarter is slow. You’re fixing old comparison pages and setting baselines nobody asked for.

By month 12, it compounds. Your comparison pages are the ones AI quotes in your category. Your review profiles stay fresh without a scramble. Your threads and videos show up when Google answers your buyers’ questions. And when a platform changes what it cites, you catch it that week.

Last month, you built the engine. Now you know where to point it.

Search gets you found. The stack gets you chosen.

#7430. Meta makes Muse agents speak

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The artificial intelligence-powered tool will be able to recognize conversation queries and respond in a voice selected by the user.

Meta is giving its Muse AI agents speaking capabilities in an effort to make them more engaging and easier to use.

Muse users will be able to select a voice for their personal artificial intelligence-powered agent and empower audio queries.

As explained by Meta: “Sometimes it’s easier to think out loud. With voice, you can talk through an idea with your Muse and let it take shape without worrying about the exact prompt.”

Meta said this should make it easier to use Muse to plan different projects, including work-related prep.

“Some things are better rehearsed out loud,” the company said. “Prepare for a job interview, run through a presentation, or talk through a pitch — hearing a response and answering in the moment makes it feel more like the real thing.”

Meta said the Muse avatar will also be able to express more as it speaks, and will use subtle expressions and gestures that match the tone of the conversation.

“It reacts while you talk, so you can tell it’s following along,” Meta said. “And you choose how present you want it to be: voice only, the avatar alongside your conversation, or full screen when you want to talk face to face.”

Users will even be able to give their Muse characters a custom voice, like giving it a New York accent or making it speak like a pirate.

Which, for some reason, Meta is convinced is something that people want, despite similar options falling flat with users previously.

Back in 2023, Meta introduced celebrity-styled AI chatbots on Messenger, which enabled users to engage with AI bots that could reply, in text form, in the style of various celebrities.

Nobody cared, and less than a year later, Meta shut this feature down due to lack of interest.

But Meta wasn’t done. In August 2024, Meta launched a limited audio version of the same, with the company paying millions of dollars to record the voices of actors such as Judi Dench, Keegan-Michael Key and Awkwafina for AI chatbots.

That didn’t resonate either. Meanwhile, The Wall Street Journal reported in April 2025 that some users had used the feature to generate explicit content voiced by these celebrities. That ultimately led to the demise of the feature before an expanded roll-out.

The addition of custom voices for Muse bots isn’t exactly the same, but even so, Meta seems very dedicated to a novelty idea that nobody else seems to care about.

Either way, users can now give their Muse agent a voice, so that they can walk around in public looking totally normal as they talk out loud to an AI character on their phone.

#7428. Agencies find AI overuse is leading to brief bloat

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

This article is part of Digiday’s coverage of its Digiday Media Buying Summit. More from the series →

The advertising world rushed to embrace generative AI. But now that agencies and advertisers have come to rely on the tech to keep up, they’re finding themselves vulnerable to its toxic byproducts.

In particular, agency leaders are finding the over-use of AI tools to write advertising briefs risks undermining the productivity and the day-to-day sanity of marketing staffers.

According to M&C Saatchi’s North American CEO, Nadja Bellan-White, over-reliance on AI for brief writing is approaching “a tipping point… It’s a little bit ridiculous.” Speaking during last week’s Digiday Media Buying Summit, she estimated that 85% of the briefs sent to the agency by clients were written using AI tools.

The impact? Corporate documents that run into the hundreds of pages, replete with marketing jargon but little actual vision. “How many many times can you say ‘framework’ in one sentence? How many times can you try ‘economies of scale’? How many times can you tell me I need this to ‘tie back to commercial objectives’?”

Brief writing has become one of the most common applications for AI tech in marketing. More than half (56.4%) of marketers and agencies now use it to build out strategy, media or campaign creative briefs, according to a survey conducted by Basis Technologies between July and August.

Media agencies use agents to suggest audience segments, run analyses of competitors’ media plans or suggest search keywords to bid on. Creative shops and influencer agencies use AI to skip through reams of consumer research, brand guidelines and economic trends, or to find ways of trumping received marketing wisdom. In-house teams at high-spending brands use generative tools to spin up strategy approaches. Even publishers now use agentic tools that respond to client briefs with AI-generated insights.

Staffers will point to the hours clawed back or to the insights discovered from a broader or deeper reading of research. Behind closed doors, however, they kvetch about the cost.

“I’ve seen some of the worst briefs I’ve ever seen in my career recently, and it’s because they’re so disjointed and there’s no through-line on what… the marketing goal is,” said one agency executive, speaking under Chatham House rules at a townhall session at DMBS.

“AI is making it worse. It’s pontificating on a sentence structure that makes [a brief] 10 pages long,” said another.

Complaints about the proliferation of memos or emails, or indeed badly written campaign briefs, aren’t new. At the start of the decade, industry veterans will recall there was even a cross-industry initiative to encourage better brief writing. But just as it’s sped up the production of digital creative assets, Claude and ChatGPT tools have enabled bad writing to spread like knotweed. As another agency exec put it: “There’s a lack of critical thinking.”

Industry leaders are beginning to acknowledge those problems in public. “[AI] can be a good sparring partner,” said Bellan-White. “But at the end of the day, you need to be the one to make the decision. You understand the client’s briefs. You understand the market context. You’ve got to really think about what it is that’s recommended.”

It’s not hard to see how AI has become a crutch. Good briefs take time to craft, time that clients are loath to grant their agencies, or to use themselves, for something so far removed from the end product. Little surprise, then, that staffers turn to a solution that does the work for them like a white-collar version of the shoemaker’s elves.

In the Brothers Grimm tale, however, the shoemaker eventually retakes control of production. But advertising staffers are long-term practitioners of what academics call “cognitive offloading,” the delegation of knowledge work to a tool or machine.

A growing body of research suggests that such over-reliance on AI tools literally reduces the cognitive abilities of users. One 2025 MIT Media Lab study, for example, measured the brainwaves of students writing essays without the aid of technology, compared with those writing with the assistance of search engines or ChatGPT. The AI-assisted group showed a 55% reduction in brainwave activity.

Whatever the name, the signs are the same. A profusion of em-dashes, paragraph upon paragraph of empty, over-long sentences, the phrase “it’s not X, it’s Y.”

Cognitive offloading isn’t just an abstract (or aesthetic) problem for ad agency leaders, some of whom are recognizing that some marketing staffers have gone from using AI as an aid to relying upon it to prop them up. Bloated documents steal time from colleagues or clients, while many users’ loose attitude to the statistics AI tools conjure up demand for a closer-than usual supervision by fact-checkers. According to a GWI survey of 150 British marketers published last month, 29% admitted inaccurate or misleading insights had cost their companies financially.

“They have exported all of their thinking to AI,” said Tony Russo, vp, innovation and strategy at indie agency Mile Marker, during another DMBS session. “It’s a judgment problem.”

If there is a solution, it’s an offline one. Christina Riccitelli, chief innovation and analytics officer at media agency OpAD, said managers should intervene if they found junior staff leaning too hard on AI. “You have to reel them back in,” she said.

Bellan-White recommended more drastic action. “Turn off your laptop. Just literally shut it down. Turn off your phones,” she said. “I want you to look me in the eye and actually have a conversation. Do you know how uncomfortable that is for people today? Because if you actually have to have a conversation, that means you actually have to know what you’re talking about.”

Advertisers now demand creator metrics like cost per lead and conversions, not follower counts.

The AI platform is testing an analytics dashboard that counts how often a business shows up in ChatGPT’s answers.

Despite leaning on creators for most of the year, marketers aren’t doing it for the holiday crunch. That job still belongs to celebrities.

#7426. Report Puts AI At 76B Monthly Sessions, Drops Search Engine Comparison via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

An updated AI usage report says it can no longer reliably compare AI used for search with search engines. AI referrals grew but stay a small share of traffic.

Graphite’s updated AI usage report puts six AI assistants at 76 billion sessions a month worldwide in September, up 37% from a year earlier. Unlike the agency’s March edition, it doesn’t compare that usage with search engines.

In March, the agency put monthly AI sessions at 56% the size of search worldwide and 34% in the U.S., with search-related AI use at 28% and 17%. The new report says that edition likely undercounted Google search use from Google’s Android app, and that the agency “can no longer reliably compare” the size of AI used for search with search engines.

The session counts are Similarweb estimates of web visits plus mobile app sessions. The report doesn’t include desktop apps because, as it explains, there isn’t reliable data available for them. Graphite sells SEO and AEO services, while Similarweb sells the data.

According to the March report, search engine usage was calculated based on website visits only (not including the apps), since the apps saw little use.

However, according to the November report, the Google Android app is different, accounting for an estimated 11.8 billion monthly sessions in the U.S. People use the app for image recognition, translation and Google Discover as well as general search. The agency says it has “no reliable data source” to determine what percent of these sessions are related to general search.

The March report’s 56% figure for total AI session usage used a web-based only count of search engines. In addition, the March report’s estimate that ChatGPT accounted for 20% of global search-related traffic used the same count. Although the new report does not revisit either of these numbers, as of this writing, the March page is still highlighting these numbers as some of the major findings from that report, though there is a link to the new report at the top.

The report’s data “suggest that AI accounts for less than 1% of traffic on average” to websites. A separate chart of U.S. traffic in the second quarter of 2026 puts organic search at 49 times the volume of AI referrals and paid search at eight times.

AI referral traffic has grown from that small base, up 92% year over year worldwide as of July and 75% in the U.S. The report’s referral figures cover the top 43,000 sites among domains with at least 100,000 monthly U.S. visits in six or more months between July 2023 and July 2026. It tracks AI referrals to those sites worldwide and in the U.S.

In July, ChatGPT accounted for 60% of AI referral traffic worldwide, followed by Gemini at 14% and Claude at 10%. In the U.S., ChatGPT’s share was 66%, while Claude accounted for 11% and Gemini for 10%.

Between July and December 2025, global session activity with the six assistants increased by 2.3%. The report describes this as a plateau. Then global activity with all the assistants rose by 19% from January through September 2026.

Year-over-year growth in U.S. session activity was 45% in September.

Worldwide session activity with ChatGPT grew 24% year over year. ChatGPT also represented 58.9% of the sessions added.

Claude had the largest increase (in percent) globally, at 1,901%. Claude also generated 26% of the additional sessions. Perplexity was the only assistant among the six to show a decline, falling 27% globally.

Most global sessions occurred on mobile (mobile app or mobile web), at 89% in the third quarter of 2026. Mobile comprised 78% of sessions in the United States.

Graphite’s data for Google in March was only from measuring the number of visits to Google’s website. The agency now says it can’t determine what percentage of the total usage of the Android app is search. OpenAI didn’t include the actual Google figure when it said that ChatGPT receives approximately one-fifth as many search-like queries as Google. I wrote about this on Nov. 3. The two estimates also count different things, with OpenAI logging a search whenever a question sends ChatGPT to the web and Graphite counting website visits and app sessions.

Before an AI-to-search ratio goes into a channel plan, check how its source counted Google.

Graphite cites anecdotal evidence that some visits prompted by AI answers get credited to direct visits or branded search, which AI referral reports wouldn’t catch. Its early numbers suggest branded search traffic is fairly flat year over year, with full results to come.

That measure is broader than the one in Similarweb’s June data, which I covered. Among people who visited a brand’s site after ChatGPT recommended it, 55.9% of that traffic came through branded search, in U.S. desktop data.

#7425. Reddit highlights opportunities for financial services marketers

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The company released TransUnion data suggesting that financial promotions in its app outperform similar campaigns on other platforms.

Reddit is making a pitch to financial marketers by highlighting data that shows how effective financial services ads are in the app.

This is probably not the first market sector that comes to mind when considering Reddit’s promotional potential for ads. But with more than 500 million weekly users, Reddit has a large audience of people exploring all kinds of topics.

As explained by Reddit: “Reddit brings together people actively seeking answers with communities built around shared experiences and expertise. For Financial Services shoppers, those conversations can play an important role in the decision journey. 62% of financial services shoppers in the UK on Reddit say that reading honest, unfiltered experiences from everyday people is an important factor when researching products or services, and 70% in Germany say Reddit helps them buy with confidence.”

In order to highlight the value of the app for financial services promotions, Reddit commissioned TransUnion to conduct a marketing mix modeling analysis of the in-app financial promotions that have run in the region comprising Europe, the Middle East and Africa.

The study showed that financial services advertisers are seeing 9 times returns on their Reddit ad spend, which the analysis said is much higher than this sector sees in other apps.

A key benefit of Reddit ads in this context is that the promotions can amplify the impact of financial services ads across other platforms.“TransUnion found that 81% of Reddit’s total impact came directly from Reddit, while 19% came from improved performance in other channels — nearly one-fifth of its impact showed up elsewhere on the media plan,” Reddit said.

The data showed that paid search drives the biggest benefit in this respect.

That makes sense, given that Reddit posts have increasingly been cited by search engines and artificial intelligence chatbot responses. As such, increasing discussion around a brand in the app would have expanded exposure potential.

However, it’s also worth noting that Reddit has seen a major decline in search referrals lately. The platform reported last week in its Q3 earnings that search referral traffic dropped by more than one million referrals on average per week in October.

That would likely reduce the expanded benefit of Reddit exposure through promotions.

Either way, Reddit could offer expanded opportunities to reach interested consumers seeking financial services info and products.

#7424. In graphic detail: Six thousand brands later, ChatGPT ads still have a conversion problem

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

ChatGPT now handles roughly a fifth of the search queries Google does. Its ads business is worth considerably less. Nobody should be surprised by that. OpenAI only started selling ads this year, the format they’re growing into is still taking shape and the company has been tiptoeing around how much advertising to put in front of users. Advertising is, in other words, lagging usage. OpenAI will want that to change quickly and advertisers are already testing how fast it can.

There’s room for OpenAI to increase the reach of its ad business within markets where it already operates. According to data from Similarweb and Graphite, the U.K. has the highest proportion of ad-eligible ChatGPT users seeing ads (45.7%), followed by the U.S. (43.4%) and Australia (43.3%).

But the data shows fewer than half of eligible users, even in OpenAI’s most established ad markets, are currently being reached by ads. In Mexico, for example, that figure falls to just 27.8%. The differences could reflect how far along each market is in the advertising rollout, or how much of its eligible audience OpenAI is currently monetizing.

The mix of advertisers spending on ChatGPT is also broadening beyond retail. According to data from Sensor Tower, shopping accounted for 38% of U.S. ad spend on the platform in April, but that share fell to 20% by September.

Over the same period, financial services increased its share of spend on ChatGPT from 2% to 13%, while software grew from 13% to 18%, and travel and tourism increased from 5% to 9%. This suggests that ChatGPT is attracting demand from a wider range of advertisers, rather than relying on a narrow range of verticals looking to reach consumers in shopping-related moments.

This has certainly broadened since the ad pilot launched in February. While Sensor Tower only started tracking ad spend in April 2026, at launch, the company estimates that around 42% of ads on ChatGPT were from advertisers in the shopping, followed by jobs & education (10%), food & dining (9%), software (8%), media and entertainment (8%) and travel (7%).

The number of brands advertising on ChatGPT is growing too. Data from Adthena shows that it tracked 1,082 distinct brands running ads on the platform, across the U.S., Australia, the U.K. and the EU in June. That number rose to 3,741 in July and 6,333 in August. And while the data for September only goes as far as Sept. 20, that full month is expected to reach around 6,830, based on Adthena’s data and projections.

It points to a growing pool of brands advertising on ChatGPT as the platform expands its markets and advertising capabilities.

New Street Research models the number of commercial chats on ChatGPT to grow from 45.9 billion this year, to nearly 380 billion by 2030, as the proportion of total chats carrying ads increases from 20% to 28% during the same period.

But the volume of ad opportunities is only part of the equation. The way those conversations are monetized will also matter. OpenAI recently said CPC and outcome-optimized bidding account for the majority of its ad campaigns, a higher proportion than New Street had previously assumed in its own model.

That could be positive for revenue, given CPC ads typically generate more per-ad event than impression-based pricing. However, New Street cautions that monetization may currently be weaker than it had originally modelled, suggesting its estimated CPC of around $5 could be too high.

That said, there is a question over whether ChatGPT ads are currently delivering enough value to advertisers to support the kind of revenue growth OpenAI is targeting. Research from a working paper under review by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze, based on data from ecommerce websites, found that paid ChatGPT visits generate $0.89 in revenue per session for U.S. advertisers, compared with $2.45 for paid Google Search visits.

The difference was also reflected in conversion rates: 0.37% for paid ChatGPT traffic, compared with 1.17% for Google. The findings suggest that while advertisers are increasingly testing the platform, OpenAI still has work to do to demonstrate that its ads can compete with established performance channels.

Those performance questions are compounded by ongoing measurement issues, according to Accuracast’s group CEO Farhad Divecha, who said the latest partner integrations — Magnite and Pubmatic — have not necessarily addressed the underlying tracking issues.

“We continue to see discrepancies there,” he said. “Some are teething problems because it’s a new system that has to be set up on advertiser systems, but some problems are down to attribution being messed up.”

Advertisers now demand creator metrics like cost per lead and conversions, not follower counts.

#7422. Meta’s AI ads included unapproved discounts

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Recent reports found that the artificial intelligence-powered ad tools posted discount offers to customers even with promotions turned off.

As artificial intelligence tools become more empowered, new parameters need to be established to limit their capacity when it comes to undertaking certain tasks.

There have already been reports of an AI tool giving out a user’s home address, generating hundreds of videos at a users’ expense and conducting questionable crypto trades.

Automated errors can also extend to buying digital ads. PPC Land reported last week that Meta’s AI-powered ad tools took discounts from a store’s website and displayed them on the business’s Facebook and Instagram ads, “even when the shop had turned promotions off on the ad it copied.”

The discovery was made by digital marketing advisor Bram Van der Hallen, who shared a LinkedIn post outlining the discovery.

As per Van der Hallen: “Meta may now automatically detect offers from your website and use them in your Meta ads. Even when you have turned off this option for your original ad. When the option to display offers detected from your website and ads is enabled in Commerce Manager, Meta may then automatically display these offers in your ads.”

Van der Hallen said the issue can be controlled by updating Commerce Manager settings to stop Meta from using detected offers in other campaigns.

But this adds another element to consider, and PPC Land noted that it could cause issues for advertisers: “This matters for any business advertising on Meta with more than one offer live, because a discount meant for one campaign or one audience could show up somewhere else.”

Meta recently outlined how its expanded processing capacity is helping generate more effective ad campaigns. The company said that improvements to its ads ranking system drove a more than 8% increase in ad clicks and a 15.7% uplift in conversions on Facebook in Q2 2026.

However, as more systems are guided by AI, there will be errors because AI systems seek out efficiencies and optimizations wherever they can, which could cause issues.

Advertisers need to be aware of these potential issues, which could have a big impact on campaign approaches.

#7421. Why Liquid Death’s media chief is determined to break away from LiveRamp

Join us Dec. 1-3 in Nashville for the Digiday Programmatic Marketing Summit

Liquid Death’s chief media officer could do without another branded hoodie this holiday season. A credible alternative to LiveRamp would go down far better.

Benoit Vatere has been looking for one since early August, when the beverage brand stopped the identity graph, after about 18 months of usage. The decision came weeks after Publicis Groupe’s plan to acquire LiveRamp was made public. In an interview with Digiday, Vatere said it was a simple choice: “I don’t want to train or have them see that super valuable information [for] anybody that I’m trying to get market share from.”

That fear stems from what LiveRamp learned about Liquid Death’s customers. The company’s job was to recognize the same people as they moved between screens and sites, so someone who saw an ad on a smart TV could be found again on a phone or a retailer’s site.

Over time that showed the brand which ads got people buying. Names and email addresses that get swept up in that tracking don’t concern Vatere since Publicis won’t see personal information. He’s far more concerned about the buying patterns. Publicis, after all, also works for brands Liquid Death competes with, like Evian and PepsiCo.

Vatere worries his patterns could end up in the data the holdco uses to train its AI tools and subsequently help make strategic calls for those rivals. Granted, the deal’s terms say that can’t happen. But Vatere expects them to change — terms and conditions get rewritten all the time, after all — not to mention the FTC’s watch over the deal lasts only five years.

“Let’s be clear about why Publicis bought LiveRamp,” continued Vatere. “They did it because there is value right? And the value is not just the revenue.”

That’s an indictment of every holdco with designs on an identity graph as it is of Publicis specifically. Vatere won’t hand his data to any company that also advises his competitors, which rules out the likes of Havas (still a LiveRamp user), WPP or Omnicom (which is building its own alternative).

In fact, Omnicom’s Acxiom has already tried its luck. Vatere sent it packing on the same grounds. “I’m not mad at Publicis. I just don’t want any of the holdcos to own it.”

That leaves independent providers, and Vatere isn’t naive about them either. Most are built with an acquisition and an exit in mind, so whichever one he picks will have to sign a contract that ends the relationship and deletes Liquid Death’s data the moment control changes hands.

“There should be a clause [that] if there’s change of ownership, change of control, contract out, right? Data deleted, like the whole thing, “ added Vatere.

He has a deadline of sorts. The LiveRamp contract runs out at the end of the year, and Liquid Death isn’t big enough to build its own graph. “I cannot do without it right now,” he said.

Chances are he won’t have to. The industry has no shortage of would-be LiveRamp replacements and plenty of them have already found their way to Vatere’s DMs. Earlier this week, the marketer posted his stance on LinkedIn after seeing reports that the holdco wasn’t concerned about competitors leaving now the deal has closed.

The replies read like a who’s who of the opportunists circling the fallout. One of them was LiveRamp’s CEO, said Vatere. He sent him a connection request, which was duly accepted. Nothing has come of it so far. Not much could. The only thing that would win him back is LiveRamp pulling out of the deal — and that ship has sailed.

Vatere is far from the only industry player to have taken this stance. LiveRamp rivals have been fielding calls and pitching for business since the deal was announced in the Spring. Both WPP and Omnicom have stopped working with the solution.

Advertisers have spent years investing heavily in cloud infrastructure, customer data platforms and first-party data infrastructure with the aim of retaining ownership of customer information as they activate media strategies. CMOs worried about maintaining that control may be at the front of the queue to speak to alternative providers.

“Advertising is an inherently zero-sum game. You need to beat your competitors to grow,” said Ruben Schreurs, CEO at Ebiquity. “Taking a uniform commoditized approach to communications or media is not a good strategy.”

“If your identity graph and your customer intelligence is your most important intellectual property, then you can’t choose infrastructure whose business model creates the appearance of conflicting incentives,” said Lai.

Schreurs argued, however, that working with LiveRamp alongside rivals won’t be the act that jeopardises a brand’s edge. “I do think it’s a little overplayed,” he said. “You can absolutely manage things in a way that if [your] agency also works for competing brands, that doesn’t necessarily have to be a problem. The same is true with LiveRamp.”

Whether any of this has a material impact on the trajectory of the business under Publicis remains uncertain. The likely answer is that Publicis wants LiveRamp’s data and connections for its own AI ambitions, combining LiveRamp’s clean room and data connectivity tech with the identity capabilities of Epsilon and the tech services of Publicis Sapient.

In any case, many of Vatere’s peers may find themselves boxed into to signing up with a Publicis-backed LiveRamp, or one of the rival holdco solutions, due to the market’s contraction in recent years.

“Clients absolutely care about conflict, how conflict is managed, but they have less and less optionality,” noted Schreurs. “There is now a big global three to choose from, so you’re going to work with a company that also works for competing brands. Then it becomes all about how you retain your competitive edge.”

Competitors and non-Publicis businesses are also a sliver of the business, accounting for roughly 5% of LiveRamp’s $800 million annual revenue.

A few defections at the edges are a price the holdco can afford to pay. Whether marketers like Vatere peel away in big enough numbers to change that sum remains an open question.

#7419. SEO Split Testing In 2027: How To Prove A Change Actually Worked

This webinar uses Conductor's research to help you prioritize marketing data and AI visibility measurement fixes.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Calls from ChatGPT and Claude often get filed as direct. This checklist shows how to track AI search as its own call source.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Guide: AI Max Drove 68% Of Retail Invalid Clicks

Before & after charts don't prove SEO results. Here's how to run an SEO split test, read the numbers and report a result your CFO will trust.

A client asked us a question recently that I wish every client asked.

We sent over a few ideas for their product pages, and one came back with a note: “If we ran this as an A/B split test, what metric would we measure it on? What are we actually trying to achieve?”

It’s a fair challenge. It’s also the one SEO has historically been the worst at answering.

For years, the standard answer has been a before-and-after chart. We changed the title tags in March, clicks went up in April, and everyone nodded. But anyone who has presented SEO results to the C-suite knows the follow-up: “How do you know that wasn’t just Google?”

In 2026, that question is harder to dodge than ever. Core updates, seasonality, and AI Overviews can all move your traffic without you touching a thing.

I’ve written this article from the agency side of the table, where proving a result is part of the job. I’ll be covering what proof actually looks like, how an SEO split test works, which method fits the site you have, and how to report a result so it survives the boardroom.

A before-and-after comparison tells you that something changed. It can’t tell you what.

Organic traffic to any group of pages is being pushed around by a lot of things at once:

Then there’s the results page itself. AI Overviews and AI Mode can change how often people click without your ranking moving at all, and Google counts that AI feature data in the overall Search Console performance report.

So the real question isn’t “did traffic go up?” It’s “did traffic go up more than it would have without the change?” That estimate is called the counterfactual, and every credible SEO test is really just a way of building one.

See also: How Do I Know If AI Overviews Are Taking Clicks From My Site And What Can I Do About It? – Ask An SEO

In my experience, a result that holds up in front of a finance team almost always has four things behind it:

That last point is exactly what our client’s question was getting at. If you choose the metric and what counts as a win after you’ve seen the data, you’ll always find a way to call it a win.

It also forces you to decide what the change is actually for. A title tag rewrite should move clicks from search. A layout change designed to help shoppers compare options is really a conversion test first, with search metrics as a guardrail.

The fix is a short brief, written, and shared before anything goes live:

It rarely needs more than a page, and it changes the final conversation from “do we believe you?” to “did it pass the test we agreed on?”

Giulia Panozzo’s recent piece on the mistakes that undermine SEO experiments goes deeper on the design side.

SEO split testing often gets confused with CRO testing, which splits users between two versions of a page. That doesn’t work for SEO.

Google only ranks one version of each URL at a time, so splitting users can’t tell you how a change affects rankings or clicks from search. And showing Googlebot different pages from the ones people see is cloaking, which Google’s guidance on website testing says is against its spam policies “whether you’re running a test or not.”

So an SEO split test splits pages instead of people. You take a group of pages built on the same template, like product, category, or location pages, and divide them into two buckets. The variant pages get the change, and the control pages stay exactly as they are.

Matched buckets. The two groups need to behave the same way before the test starts. Keep pages that compete for the same queries together as one unit, or a winning variant can simply take clicks from its control twin.

Then match units by traffic level and category and randomly assign them. Some platforms automate the balancing, like SearchPilot’s smart bucketing.

A concurrent run. Both groups run over the same dates, so a core update or a holiday spike lands on both at the same time. That doesn’t guarantee they’ll react the same way, since an update can hit some categories harder than others. That’s why the matching and the check below matter.

A forecast. The control group is used to model what the variant pages would have done without the change. The gap between that forecast and what actually happened is your result.

A pre-launch check. Pick a few pretend launch dates in the past, train the model on the data before each one, and see how well it predicts the weeks after, using windows the same length as your test. If it keeps “finding” effects in periods where nothing happened, it won’t be able to tell you what your change did.

Google’s open-source CausalImpact package is the best-known model for building that forecast. SearchPilot started out on it before moving to a neural network model in 2019 so it could pick up smaller uplifts.

Not every site can run a textbook split test. SearchPilot’s rule of thumb is that the section you’re testing should get around 1,000 organic visits per day.

Below that, tests tend to drag on or never reach a clear answer. That doesn’t mean smaller sites can’t test. It means choosing the right design and being honest about how strong the evidence is.

If you’re limited to a pre/post comparison, you can still make it far more defensible:

The tooling follows the same split. Enterprise platforms like SearchPilot and seoClarity’s SEO & AEO Split Tester handle deployment and modeling, SEOTesting.com runs Search Console-based tests for smaller sites, and CausalImpact is free if you have data support in-house. If your CMS already lets you change a subset of pages on a template, you may not need a platform for your first few tests.

A good SEO split test report only needs a handful of numbers.

Uplift against the forecast. The difference between what the variant pages did and what the model expected. It’s your headline, but it should never appear on its own.

The interval. The range of effects the model considers plausible. Bayesian tools call it a credible interval and others a confidence interval, but either way, if it includes zero, the result doesn’t show a positive effect.

Probability of a positive effect. This is the easiest number for non-technical stakeholders to follow, but check what your tool is reporting. CausalImpact’s “probability of a causal effect” doesn’t say which direction, so a confident loss can score as high as a win.

Be careful with framing, too. A 90% probability of a positive effect still leaves a one in ten chance the change did nothing or made things worse.

Revenue or conversions on the tested pages. The number that turns an SEO result into a business case. Revenue is noisier than clicks, so treat it as directional if volumes are small.

Rankings can help explain why clicks moved, but compare them against the control group too. They’re never proof on their own.

See also: Reporting Uncertainty Without Losing Credibility

Google says Search Console’s Search Generative AI performance reports rolled out to all sites on Aug. 31, 2026, although sites with too few AI impressions won’t see one. The reports show how often your pages appeared in AI Overviews and AI Mode, broken down by page.

So you can compare AI feature impressions for your variant and control groups, the same way you would click. If a change lifts clicks but loses AI visibility, or the other way around, that’s worth digging into before you roll out.

There’s no click data yet, so treat it as a supporting signal. And if you’re using rankings as supporting evidence, remember that every link in an AI Overview is given the position of the AI Overview itself, as Google’s John Mueller recently confirmed.

Here’s what a clean test looks like from start to finish. The numbers are illustrative, but this is the shape you want before you face a CFO.

The change. A new title tag and meta description template for product pages, rewritten to lead with what the shopper is searching for instead of the brand name.

The brief. The primary metric is non-branded organic clicks, and conversion rate can’t fall more than 2% relative to control. The smallest lift worth acting on is 5%, and the analysis date is six weeks after launch. The template rolls out only if the 95% interval sits entirely above zero, the central estimate clears 5%, and the guardrail holds.

The split. 400 product pages, clustered so pages competing for the same queries stay together, then matched by traffic level and category and randomly assigned. That gives roughly 200 variant and 200 control pages, and the setup passes the pre-launch check.

The result. At six weeks, variant pages get 14.2% more non-branded organic clicks than the forecast built from the control group, with a 95% credible interval of 8% to 19%. The model puts the probability of a positive effect at over 99%, and the conversion data rules out a drop beyond the 2% guardrail.

The interval first clears zero on day 27. The test still runs to the agreed six-week mark, and the effect holds.

The business outcome. Organic revenue from sessions landing on the variant pages comes in 9.6% above its own forecast. Its interval is much wider than the click result, so it’s reported as directional. Average position on target terms moves from 6.4 to 4.8 while the control group holds steady, which helps explain where the extra clicks came from.

The decision. The template rolls out to the remaining product pages. From then on, you’re monitoring that the gain persists, since there’s no longer a control group to prove it.

Most tests won’t look this tidy. In 2024, SearchPilot re-ran what it called a representative sample of past tests through its newest model, and 29% came back positive at 95% confidence, up from 13% with its previous best model.

So even with a purpose-built model, most of those tests didn’t show a significant win. That doesn’t mean the changes did nothing, but it’s worth knowing before you push something sitewide.

Lead with the decision, not the methodology. Most stakeholders want to know three things: what you’re recommending, how sure you are, and what it’s worth.

A one-page report that covers this usually looks like:

The recommendation: Roll out, roll back, or record it as inconclusive.

The result in one sentence: “Our model estimates the new template lifted non-branded clicks to the tested product pages by between 8% and 19%.”

What it’s worth: Revenue or leads on the tested pages, plus a rollout projection with its assumptions spelled out.

How you tested it: The pages, split, dates, and method, plus anything that happened during the test, like a core update.

For the projection, start from the conservative end of the range, spell out how the remaining pages differ from the tested ones and call it a scenario, not a result. If the full rollout beats a conservative number, you build trust. If it misses an optimistic one, you lose it.

And report the losers. A test log that only contains wins looks like cherry-picking, because it is. Sharing negative and inconclusive results is what makes the wins believable.

Monitor daily to catch implementation problems, but make the call on the planned analysis date, unless your platform uses a method built for continuous monitoring. Calling a test the first time it crosses the line makes it much more likely you’ll roll out a false positive.

Some tools apply changes with JavaScript. Use the URL Inspection tool to confirm the change appears in the rendered HTML, and check the variant pages have been recrawled since it went live.

For title tests, also check what Google is actually showing. Google rewrites title links when it thinks it has a better option, so the title you’re testing isn’t always the one searchers see.

The client who asked what metric we’d measure wasn’t being difficult. They were holding SEO to the same standard as every other channel in their budget.

Split testing won’t make every change a winner. Plenty won’t be. What it does is replace “trust us” with a result your stakeholders can check for themselves.

Write the brief before you start, compare against a fair control, report a range instead of a single number, and tie it back to revenue. Do that consistently, and “how do you know that wasn’t just Google?” becomes a question you can actually answer.

#7418. Revenue Accounting Manager at LiveKit

LiveKit is building the infrastructure layer for the voice-driven era of computing. Our platform gives developers everything they need to build, test, deploy, scale, and observe agents in production. Founded in 2021, LiveKit powers voice AI applications for OpenAI, xAI, Salesforce, Coursera, Spotify, and thousands of others, collectively facilitating billions of calls each year.

Our revenue is credit-denominated and consumption-based — usage billing, prepaid credit drawdown, and concurrency pricing across a growing enterprise base — which is close to the most complex revenue profile in infrastructure software. The load-bearing questions are open and there are few set policies and processes.

You will be the technical authority on revenue. You will own the entire Order to Cash cycle, from interfacing with our sales team, reviewing contracts, assessing terms in accordance with ASC 606, implementing workpapers and schedules, documenting conclusions, and assisting with billing and collection efforts. If building processes from square one and taking ownership of some of the most complex revenue arrangements excites you, this is the role for you.

You'll thrive as a Revenue Accounting Manager if you:

are obsessed with making the best product for our customers

are known as the go-to person for tackling tough problems

are focused on polish, detail and quality

are a fast learner, frequently picking up new tips, tricks, and skills

The best way to impress us is with thoughtful ways you'd implement LiveKit, and potentially tinkering with it 😊

Author our revenue accounting policy set — principal versus agent on brokered inference, breakage on expiring credits, performance obligation identification and allocation, minimum commitment versus overage, and contract modifications — and make each one stand up to an external auditor

Own the monthly revenue close: recognition, the deferred revenue rollforward, contract asset and liability balances, and the flux analysis

Own the revenue portion of our external audit, from the PBC list through the technical positions

Replace manual revenue entries with an automated billing-to-revenue reconciliation and a documented exception process — revenue should be computed by a system and reviewed by a person, with invoice accuracy above 99% and root-cause tracking on the misses

Govern order to cash: billing accuracy, dispute resolution, and an AR and collections process with real DSO and aging targets

Own commission capitalization and amortization under ASC 340-40

Review non-standard deal structures before they're signed, so the accounting consequence is a decision rather than a discovery

You're a licensed CPA with a Big 4 or comparable technical accounting foundation, plus real industry experience in a high-growth startup environment

You have demonstrable ASC 606 experience with usage-based or consumption revenue

You write technical memos that a reviewer can follow without a meeting: facts, guidance, analysis, conclusion

Experience assessing GAAP guidance and implementing it in real-world situations

You've owned a monthly revenue close hands-on, and you've closed revenue through at least one external audit

You're comfortable being the technical authority without a bench behind you

Billing system implementation or migration — Metronome, Stripe, Zuora

Enough SQL to validate a recognition schedule against raw usage data yourself

An opportunity to build something truly impactful to the world

Contribute to open source alongside world-class engineers

#7417. YouTube expands custom feeds and offers new partnership options

Let Social Media Today's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The platform is trying to make it easier for users to access personally relevant discovery options using artificial intelligence-enabled responses.

YouTube updated its in-app discovery listings and also integrated its artificial intelligence-powered Ask Studio guidance with its support tools to make it easier to manage queries in a single workflow. The company is also testing product recommendations for potential creator partnerships.

First, YouTube is expanding its custom feed listings in order to make it easier for users to create and access personally relevant feeds based on conversational prompts.

Currently available to U.S. users, YouTube’s custom feed generation option provides another way to define the in-app experience by enabling users to tell YouTube’s AI system what they want to see.

YouTube is now making these custom feeds easier to access by adding them to the top navigation bar.

These custom feeds will also replace non-custom topic options in the top listing. YouTube's also moving the subscription and standard feed options, bringing them together into the top-of-feed display.

That should make it easier for users to integrate this AI-powered option and help them build a more personally relevant in-app experience.

For creators, YouTube is rolling out an integrated Ask Studio and YouTube Help chat element. This should make it easier for creators to generate AI guidance for their channel and connect with YouTube’s internal support for other queries.

YouTube’s Head of Editorial Rene Ritchie said this will mean that creators no longer have to switch between chat windows for each element.

YouTube is also testing product recommendations for brand content partnerships. These are personalized to each channel and could help creators find more relevant sponsorship opportunities.

As explained by Ritchie: “If you're an eligible affiliate creator, YouTube Studio is rolling out a brand new personalized product recommendation shelf right inside your shopping hub. These recommendations are based on your channel's past content and audience engagement and what's trending in your niche, like beauty, tech, or home.”

The new display will also show estimated commission rates for each potential partnership, providing more assistance for creators when considering their opportunities.

Finally, YouTube is expanding its Hype with Jewels creator donation option to more markets.

This is a combination of two products: YouTube’s Jewels are essentially an in-app currency that viewers can use to buy in-app digital stickers, which they can then send to creators to show their support during a livestream.

Users can purchase packages of Jewels, and creators get a cut from any sticker allocated during their stream.

YouTube’s Hype program, meanwhile, enables viewers to allocate Hype points to a video in order to boost its ranking and help it get seen by more people.

Hype with Jewels lets creators use purchased Jewels to add more Hype to videos, which will then help them get seen by more people.

As per YouTube: “Starting November 6, 2026, we’re expanding Hype with Jewels to eligible creators and viewers in the United States, Canada, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Poland, Spain, Turkey, and the United Kingdom.”

YouTube is also expanding the Hype limits for streams, with viewers now able to allocate as much Hype as they like to streamers.
